utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then it is so ordered. We are in private session, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.text: Not yet. Now we are. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Very good. Then shall we go back into public session at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar? (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would draw the Appellate Chamber's decision to paragraph 6.5 of our brief regarding ground 5, wherein we state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is that 6.5?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It is 6.5, Your Honour. Wherein we state that the witness statements' decision is directly contradicted by more recent practice at the Trial Chamber level, and we cite to a decision in the Dokmanovic case. On further reflection, Your Honours, the Prosecution would withdraw that paragraph because it appears to us that the Dokmanovic decision does not directly contradict the Trial Chamber decision in this case. The Dokmanovic decision was issued for reasons entirely separate, having to do with being able to ensure a trial without undue delay and to ensure to the accused a right to a fair and expeditious trial; and as set forth in the decision, the Trial Chamber wanted documents from the Defence primarily for the purpose of trial management and to promote a better comprehension of the issues that the Trial Chamber would face. Therefore, it was a decision rendered for entirely different purposes, and we do not wish to mislead the Appellate Chamber. We do not believe that it directly contradicts the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, that is entirely in the spirit of the bar, and I take it, Mr. Clegg, you offer no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Clegg, are you ready to open your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. We have you down for two hours. That is a maximum period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: A minimum. Could I begin by indicating to Your Honours that I will be dealing with the first four grounds of the Prosecution's appeal in the order in which they presented their submissions to the Appeals Chamber, and Mr. Livingston will be dealing with the fifth ground. Turning first to ground 1. In our submission, in order to determine whether victims enjoy the protection of Article 2 of the Tribunal Statute, it is necessary to determine whether they were protected persons under the Geneva Convention. Article 4 of the IV Geneva Convention states that: "(Protected persons) ... are those who ... find themselves in case of a conflict or occupation, in the hands of a Party to the conflict or Occupying Power of which they are not nationals." It follows that a number of questions need to be determined in deciding whether any individual enjoys protection under Article 2. The first question, that which has exercised the Court most anxiously, is: What is the appropriate test to be applied in order to answer the question, "Is this an international conflict?" A second and, to some extent, related question is: Can you have an international conflict and an internal conflict in the same jurisdiction at the same time? Then the third question is: Applying the facts as found by the Trial Chamber to the correct test, was there an international or an internal conflict in the region of the former Yugoslavia that we are concerned with in this appeal after the 19th of May of 1992? Turning then, if I may, to the first question, namely, what is the appropriate test to be applied in order to answer the question "Is this an international conflict?" The Prosecution has submitted that the correct test is the demonstrable link test. That test is a wide test and would embrace all situations covered by the more restrictive effective control test or a very similar but differently described agency test. In our submission, the proper test is the effective control test, and the demonstrable link test is the wrong test. It was conceded yesterday by Mr. Fenrick that there is no authority to support the demonstrable link test that he submits is the correct test to apply. We rely upon the absence of authority because we submit that there is authority to support the effective control test that we submit is the correct test. It is, we submit, implicit in the submission of the Prosecution that the reasoning of the Appeals Chamber in the interlocutory appeal on jurisdiction in the Tadic case applied the wrong reasoning in its judgement. We submit that that judgement proceeded on the effective control test. We draw attention to paragraph 76 of the judgement of the Appeals Chamber in which the judgement refers in the following terms to the question that we are now addressing: "If the Security Council had categorised the conflict as exclusively international and, in addition, had decided to bind the International Tribunal thereby, it would follow that the International Tribunal would have to consider the conflict between Bosnian Serbs and the central authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina as international. Since it cannot be contended that the Bosnian Serbs constitute a State, arguably the classification just referred to would be based on the implicit assumption that the Bosnian Serbs are acting not as a rebellious entity but as organs or agents of another State, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia-Montenegro). As a consequence, serious infringements of international humanitarian law committed by the government army of Bosnia-Herzegovina against Bosnian Serb civilians in their power would not be regarded as grave breaches ..." Now, the important words used by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic interlocutory appeal are, in our submission, "as organs or agents of another State." If somebody is the organ or the agent of another state, in our submission, that is another way of expressing the effective control test. The Appeals Chamber judgement is not couched in language that is consistent with a demonstrable link test. Therefore, we submit that the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Tadic case is authority to support the effective control test. We would also submit that the Nicaragua decision is also consistent with the effective control test. Mr. Fenrick strove manfully yesterday to seek to distinguish the Nicaragua case from the facts of this case. The reason for such heroic efforts was, of course, a recognition, in our submission, that if no distinction in truth exists, then that is also authority for the effective control test. Third, of persuasive force, the Encyclopaedia of Public International Law also asserts that that is the appropriate test. So our starting point is that there is a complete absence of authority to support the proposition advanced by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, the transcript would have a precise reference to the Encyclopaedia of Public International Law to which you're referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It does. It's at page 461 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. We'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Line 15. The first proposition is that there is conceded to be a complete absence of authority to support the Prosecution's assertion that a demonstrable link is all that is necessary. We submit that there is clear authority, including authority from this Appeals Chamber, supporting the effective control test. The second approach embraces the concept of state responsibility. The grave breach provisions of the Geneva Convention also embrace state responsibility. We would submit that a state can only be responsible as a consequence of a human being or human beings acting as the agent of the state. The state isn't capable of acting independently of the people who control it. If the effective control test were to be applied, then it is easy to see how the concept of state responsibility can be catered for under the same test, because if the state is in effective control of the grave breach provisions, then it is clearly right that the state should be responsible for those actions. Therefore, the principle of state responsibility would, we would submit, in equity be legitimate to be dealt with under the convention. However, if you were to adopt the test propounded by the Prosecution and adopt the demonstrable link test, that would, in our submission, be a wholly inappropriate test to embrace the concept of state responsibility. Demonstrable link obviously falls significantly short of effective control, and the result would be that states would be liable to be held responsible for the actions of other states or entities over which they did not have any effective control. That would, in our submission, result in an unjust conclusion for the states. Third, we would submit that the demonstrable link test will introduce an element of uncertainty into an area of international law which ought to be capable of clear and precise definition. The effective control test is one that it is capable to apply in any situation. By having regard to the evidence in the case, one can answer the question "Is there effective control being exercised by an outside entity or state over the forces engaged in this conflict?" That is a question that is capable of being answered by reference to the evidence in any situation one cares to imagine. It is a question that will be answered on the evidence and it can be applied equally to all situations. It is, to some extent, the mirror of what one might have in most of the criminal jurisdictions of the world, namely, the agency principle whereby if you instruct someone or employ somebody to carry out a contract killing, then you are as much guilty of murder as if you had pulled the trigger yourself. It's a concept of agency that, expressed differently, is elevated and adapted to the international arena. But as a legal concept, it is no stranger, we would submit, to the lawyers of most jurisdictions. The demonstrable link test, in our submission, has the following frailties: First, how much of a link, how much of a connection is necessary in order to elevate the crimes to grave breaches? The Prosecution in the course of their submission said, in terms, "Well, of course, not just any financial or logistical support would be sufficient," although financial and logistical support is, in English, a demonstrable link. So if that's not sufficient, what is and where do you draw the line? Applying the Prosecution's test, there will inevitably be a substantial grey area. Applying the effective control test, there is a no grey area. A simple decision of fact has to be made: Is there or is there not effective control? The Prosecution sought to draw an analogy with the lend/lease scheme between the United States of America and the United Kingdom during the Second World War. The effect of that scheme was that the United States of America, in reality, were financing the war against Germany. They gave the United Kingdom not just the money to pay our troops; they made the bullets that we could fire and the bombs that we could drop. I ask the question rhetorically: If one applied a demonstrable link, is somebody who finances and arms a side to a conflict not demonstrably linked to the party engaged in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, we must remember that scholars will be reading the transcripts 50 years hence, so when you identify the lend/lease arrangements with the United Kingdom, that could lend, I believe, itself to some degree of confusion. When you speak of "we" in that connection, perhaps there would be some prudence in remembering that you're appearing for Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Indeed, yes. I apologise. In addressing the first question, namely, what is the appropriate test to be applied, in our submission, the appropriate test is the effective control test. It has the support of authority, it provides the international arena with a clear and easy-to-apply statement of the law, and the alternative is uncertain, unsupported by authority and, we would submit, for those reasons, undesirable. May I move to consider the second question, namely: Can you have an international conflict and an internal conflict at the same time? In our submission, it is perfectly possible, in the region of the former Yugoslavia, namely Bosnia, to have an international conflict in the south between, for example, the Croats and the Muslims, where there has been proved to be direct involvement of Croatian troops, making it an international conflict, and, at the same time, in a wholly separate region in the north of Bosnia, a separate but internal conflict between the indigenous Serb population against the indigenous Muslim population. Indeed, in our submission, it would be absurd to alter the categorisation of the conflict in the north, in the example that I have just given, from a national to an international conflict as a consequence of the outbreak of a wholly separate and distinct international conflict between separate parties in a separate region. It would render the classification of conflict to chance as to whether a separate conflict occurred in a different part of the country of a different category. Perhaps, if I could, one reference, both from the transcript yesterday and from the earlier judgement to illustrate this point. It is our submission that, with respect, the approach of the Prosecution was, in part, contradictory so far as this aspect of their submission was concerned. At page 134, the Prosecution submitted, by reference to the Celebici decision, the following quotation: "Should the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina be international, the relevant norms of international humanitarian law apply throughout its territory until the general cessation of hostilities unless it can be shown that the conflicts in some areas were separate internal conflicts unrelated to the larger international conflict." So that is a quotation clearly supporting the proposition that I have just made to the Court. That quotation is adopted by the Prosecution at page 134. But by page 147, you have a slightly differently-phrased approach, where the Prosecution submit: "'Well, you can have an international armed conflict going on in this little corner of Bosnia, but up here at this end, here you still don't have the umbrella "international armed conflict" applying.' To me, the law applies to -- once you have an international armed conflict, it applies to the whole territory." Well, that, if it was intended to be a proposition contrary to the one advanced in the Celebici decision, is, in our submission, one that is without the benefit of authority. It is also, we would submit, contrary to the view expressed by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic interlocutory appeal at paragraph 72 on page 39, where the Court held: "To the extent that the conflicts had been limited to clashes between Bosnian Government forces and Bosnian Serb rebel forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as between the Croatian Government and Croatian Serb rebel forces in ... Croatia, they have been internal (unless direct involvement of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ... could be proven) --" I'm sorry, I have read the wrong highlighted passage. I am very grateful to Mr. Livingston. It is, in fact, slightly earlier in the passage, where the judgement refers to: " ... conflicts in the former Yugoslavia could have been characterised as both internal and international, or alternatively, as an internal conflict alongside an international one." So there is clearly there the recognition by the Appeals Chamber that you can have both at the same time when they use the words "an internal conflict alongside an international one." The other quotation, not without interest, because that is another reference to the direct involvement that would be necessary to be proven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Celebici passage which you read use the words, I think, "unless it can be shown." Would it be your contention that the showing has to be by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did Celebici go on to explain by whom the showing had to be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It didn't say so explicitly, no. We would submit that the establishment that the conflict is international is one of the fundamental ingredients of the offence alleging grave breaches, and therefore, it is incumbent upon the Prosecution to place before the Trial Chamber evidence that would enable the Trial Chamber to draw the conclusion of fact that the evidence was international from evidence that it presents normally through the mouths of expert witnesses, but it must be something -- in our submission, it must be proved through evidence in the absence of some admission or concession. If one reflects on the Rajic case, there there was an international conflict because it was proved that there was direct involvement of Croatian soldiers in the fighting, so the basis upon which the Trial Chamber in that case came to the conclusion that there was an international conflict is founded on the facts presented by the Prosecution in the trial process, and the contradistinction between that and this case is that, in our submission, when applying the appropriate test to the facts, the Prosecution were not able to establish that effective control was being exercised in this case over the forces that were engaged in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What do you make of the principle to which you invited attention, as flowing from the jurisprudence of this Chamber, that if there is proof of external armed intervention in a state, the presumption is that there is an international conflict throughout the territory of that state without any temporal or geographical limitations?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: There are two parts, I think, to the question posed. If there is proof of external armed intervention, I think one could assume from the use of those words that that would have embraced effective control because you couldn't have external armed intervention without effective control. Difficult to imagine. So you would have there, clearly, an international conflict in relation to the conflict that the external armed forces were engaged in, but we would not accept that there is any jurisprudence to support the assertion that that international conflict extends throughout the territory of that state without any geographical limitation. Indeed, we would submit that the jurisprudence suggests to the contrary. In the Appeals Chamber decision in the Tadic case, it was recognised in terms that, paragraph 72: "... the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia could have been ... an internal conflict alongside an international (conflict)." So that statement of principle is, we would submit, directly contrary to the proposition just adumbrated by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, I adumbrated it without reference to the documentation which I lamentably do not have before me, but it was my impression that somewhere in the decision of this Chamber in the Tadic jurisdiction case, the Trial Chamber might have said, so I think, that if there is proof of external armed intervention in the territory of a state, the implication was that that led to an international armed conflict without any temporal or geographical limitations. So that the juridical problem which that presented was how to reconcile that with these other dicta to the effect that there could be an international armed conflict alongside an internal one. I have no doubt that there can be that. But I wanted to know how you might want to reconcile the two propositions if I was right in recalling what was said in the Tadic jurisdiction case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I think the way that we would advance our submission is that if there were external armed intervention, then there would clearly be an international conflict, and that international conflict would embrace all of the conflict that was connected with or embraced by the external armed intervention, and that would cover the whole of the area, and there may well be a presumption that the fighting in the area was clearly a part of that international conflict. I am not seeking to advance a submission that one should examine the war skirmish by skirmish in order to determine whether there is an international armed conflict. That would be an absurd approach. Clearly once there is an international -- let me just rephrase that. Certainly where there is external intervention, then that will render all of the conflict international unless there is a wholly distinct and separate conflict that is internal in its nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What I would have welcomed your assistance on is on this problem: If there is a principle of law, as I believe there is, that given there is proof of external armed intervention, the implication is that the conflict is international with respect to the whole of the territory, without geographical or temporal limitations, then on whom is the burden of proof to establish that nevertheless the conflict was compartmentalised in the sense that alongside with the international conflict there was an internal conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: We would submit that once the issue was raised, then the burden would be on the Prosecution. If one drew an analogy in domestic criminal jurisdiction, certainly in the common law, if the Defence raised the defence of self-defence, by way of illustration, then the burden is then on the Prosecution to disprove it. We would submit that once the Defence have raised the issue of the conflict being internal, there would have to be some evidential basis to raise it, it couldn't be raised in a vacuum, but once raised, then the Prosecution would have the burden of proving that that part of the conflict was not a separate internal conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Clegg. I understand your position now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Can I move then to consider applying the correct test: Was the conflict with which the Appeals Chamber was seized national or international? Obviously, the answer to the question depends upon the test. If any demonstrable link were sufficient to alter the category of conflict from internal to international, then I would have to concede the evidence disclosed that there was a link existing between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Bosnian Serbs. However, we would submit that if you applied the correct test, namely, that of effective control, then the conclusion of the majority of the Trial Chamber was correct and that the Prosecution have not proved to the necessary standard that effective control existed, and we submit that that is a decision that they made based on the evidence that they heard and it is a decision that they could reasonably have come to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, should I understand you could mean this, that you concede that there was a link between Yugoslavia and the VRS and that, accordingly, you also concede that if the applicable test is, as contended by the Prosecution, a demonstrable link, then the conflict would be international?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I do make that concession with the only caveat on the assumption that any demonstrable link is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. In our submission, the decision of the Trial Chamber does not, in any sense, bind any other Trial Chamber. All that the Trial Chamber has done in the Tadic case is to conclude that the Prosecution has not presented sufficient evidence to discharge the burden on them to prove that in this case there was effective control exercised by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It does not mean that in a different case with better evidence they might not be able to prove that. All it's saying is that in this case, on this evidence, they didn't prove it. In our submission, it is not right to seek to elevate the trial decision in this case to some binding authority that is going to operate hereafter in every other case. It's a matter of proof, and the evidence may vary in different cases. Here we submit that the Prosecution did not prove to the necessary standard that effective control existed. Even Judge McDonald, in her dissenting judgement, conceded at paragraph 8 that there was little evidence that the VRS was formally under the command of Belgrade after the 19th of May, 1992. At page 227 in the main judgement, the majority -- at page 227, not paragraph 227, paragraph 607, the majority formed the view that: "... after the 19 May 1992 the armed forces of Republika Srpska could not be considered as the de facto organs or agents of the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) either in opstina Prijedor or more generally." That is a conclusion they formed on the facts, and it was, in our submission, entirely open to them to have formed that conclusion when you study the evidence of Colonel Selak who was the expert whom the Prosecution called to deal with the matter by way of expert evidence. It is entirely consistent, in our submission, with a critical analysis of his evidence for the majority of the Trial Chamber to have formed that view. By using those words, "organs or agents of the government," they are echoing the very words of the Appeals Chamber in the interlocutory appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask you this question: The majority held that the VRS was not under the control of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In coming to that conclusion, to what extent did the majority rely on the proposition that there could not be effective control unless it was proved that the VRS was under the command and control of what was left of the JNA in the Federal Republic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: My understanding of the judgement is that reliance was placed on that by the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you consider that that was an applicable criterion?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It was one of the applicable criterion, not the only one. The distinction, in our submission, is between allies who are cooperating, maybe providing financial assistance to each other and maybe sharing the same objective, and effective control. The mere fact that you have an ally who is with whom you share a common objective, not saying that that's necessary, but let's assume that it was, that you are sharing a common objective and you are allies, that would not mean that one was exercising effective control over the other, even if one were to provide the other financial support or logistical support or perhaps information. The crucial difference, in our submission, is whether one side is effectively controlling the other so that it is operating as if it were an organ of the other entity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, in that model, assuming that one ally does not have control over the other ally but assuming that they are allies and that they are prosecuting an integrated battle plan, would the use of armed force by one ally be attributable to the other ally?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: "No" would be my instinctive answer. There would be no control, and in the absence of control, there can't be responsibility. You might agree with what your ally is doing, but you're not responsible for their actions unless you join in with the action yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are you proposing to address the problem raised by Mr. Fenrick as to there being a distinction between the attribution of international responsibility to a state and the allocation of individual criminal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I was hoping to embrace part of that argument when dealing with a later ground, but it causes me no difficulty to touch on it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It's perhaps important just to remind ourselves that, of course, the fact that somebody is not a protected person under Article 2 does not mean that those responsible for war crimes against those people go unpunished, and, indeed, no one suggests that that is the position. So individual responsibility remains. One's merely looking at whether it falls under Article 2, which embraces an element of state responsibility as well and, for that reason, amongst others, must be limited to situations where the state has effective control over the actions of the individuals responsible for perpetrating the war crimes. In part, I think that deals with the question that Mr. Fenrick was raising yesterday, and I will deal with his argument or his response really to questions from the bench as to whether somebody acting for purely personal motives would still be caught by the provisions and whether there's a need for discriminatory intent a little later. If you could just give me one moment, please, Your Honours. May I turn to ground 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, the voices have indicated that the judgement of the bench is that it may be a convenient time for the coffee break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: You would have to be a braver advocate than I to disagree with that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Court will stand adjourned until, let us say, 11.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Can I begin by giving the full reference to the encyclopaedia quotation? I'm grateful to Mr. Fenrick for providing me with the answer. It's the Encyclopaedia of Public International Law, 1982, volume 4 at page 294 to 298. May I now turn to ground 3 and begin by responding to the question posed by the bench as to whether the matter falls for determination at all in light of the acknowledged position that it does not come under Article 25(1)(a) of the Tribunal's Statute. In our submission, this cannot be a ground of appeal as such. There's no provision in the Statute for the Appeals Chamber to make a declaratory judgement of the relevant law for the assistance of future Trial Chambers. There is, however, a route whereby this Appellate Chamber could express an opinion either in favour or against the statement of law decided by the Trial Chamber. In our submission, in giving judgement, this Appeals Chamber is entitled to comment on any related aspect of law, and it would be a curious appellate jurisdiction that had to be constrained to the pleadings of the parties. The comments may well strictly be described as obiter dictum, but they would nonetheless have the force of obiter from the Appeals Chamber. They would not form part of the ratio decidendi of the decision but would be persuasive authority for the future. We would have no objection to the Appeals Chamber approaching the matter in that way. It has perhaps conveniently been labelled a ground of appeal because there was nothing else to call it in the drafting stage prior to the hearing of the appeal. Strictly, we submit, it's not a ground of appeal but it raises a matter upon which the Court is invited to express an opinion, and we don't wish to discourage the Court from taking that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, we're grateful to you for your assistance on the point. I think that in paragraph 139, as I remember it, of the Tadic jurisdiction matter, you will find that what happened there was that a party withdrew a point of argument but that notwithstanding the withdrawal, the Court proceeded to pronounce upon the point because of its importance. Would that be a similar situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The same proposition, of course, applies to ground 5. Dealing now with the merits of the third ground of appeal, as I shall continue to call it for convenience sake, we submit that the Trial Chamber was correct in holding that crimes against humanity cannot be committed purely for personal motives. As I understood the submissions of Mr. Fenrick in the heat of questioning from the bench, it seems that he was forced back to a proposition which, when analysed, would result in the following conclusion: In the area of Bosnia, with which we are concerned, if a Bosnian Serb wife murdered her Bosnian Muslim husband, she would be guilty of a crime against humanity if her motives were purely personal. If the lady had been more selective with the ethnic origin of her husband, then she would not have committed any crime against humanity at all. That appeared to be the logical conclusion of the proposition being advanced by Mr. Fenrick. In our submission, reflecting on that as a result would render the proposition absurd. We don't suggest, of course, that where a crime contains an element of personal motive it is sufficient to escape liability. The important words are "purely personal motive." In other words, it must be the exclusive motive. Many cases will have mixed motives, and the perpetrators of crimes may exploit the political situation and use that as an opportunity to exact revenge where, without the conflict, no opportunity would have existed. In such a case, the perpetrator would embrace the conflict, and his motives would become mixed because he would then be committing his crime not for purely personal reasons but also because, taking the example from some of the authorities, the victim was a Jew and he knew that because of his Jewish race, he would be able to adopt, as his own, the motive of those engaged in the conflict to exploit and take advantage of the situation in such a way as to enable him to achieve an end that he would not otherwise have been able to do. I'm not suggesting for a moment that the existence of an element of personal animosity between the perpetrator of a crime and its victim will excuse his guilt as somebody responsible for a crime against humanity. The vast majority of cases, in reality, will have a mixed motive. They will be partly personal and partly embracing the motives of the conflict. But where there is crime, and there inevitably will be, that is purely personal - and I chose the analogy of what some may describe in shorthand as a domestic murder - it would be absurd if the classification of the action of the killing spouse was dependent upon the religion of his or her partner. The authorities, in our submission, do not assist the Prosecution when properly analysed. We would submit that the cases from the Second World War do not advance the proposition that a crime against humanity cannot occur if the criminal is motivated by purely personal motives because, in those cases, the criminals adopted and made their own the motives of national socialism in seeking to achieve the final solution in order to admittedly achieve some personal benefit, at times financial, at times it may be revenge. So they are, in our submission, illustrations of cases that were correctly and rightly treated as crimes against humanity, but they were so treated because they were examples of a criminal having mixed motives, his own motive for personal enrichment and the motives of national socialism which he adopted and made his own in order to achieve his other end. There is, in our submission, a distinction between such an example and one that I have given this morning of the wife killing her husband, where the motives, in my example, would be purely personal. In those circumstances, we submit, there is no reason in the application of law as to why the offence ought to be treated as a crime against humanity, there is nothing that ought to elevate it above the ordinary jurisdiction that it would otherwise fall to be determined under, and we would submit that the Trial Chamber came to the right conclusion on that issue. Insofar as other cases, such as The United States v. Altstoetter and the Attorney General v. Eichmann are concerned, by way of illustration, it is true that there no mention was there made about the necessity for a crime against humanity not to involve purely personal motives. That is because everybody accepted that if the crimes were committed by the people accused in those cases, then nobody could conceivably suggest that they were for purely personal motives. So the absence of such commentary, in our submission, is irrelevant. Those are our submissions on ground 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Clegg. You have concluded your response. Do be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not finished yet. There is ground 4 next. I was only pausing because normally, at that point in one's submissions, one receives a very probing and occasionally unwelcome question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me see if my colleagues wish to probe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I am not encouraging such a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I think it is a good opportunity for me to say to you something which I believe is well understood, that any statements made by members of the Bench are of a purely provisional nature; they are not expressive of any firm conclusions. That is understood, I believe, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Certainly it has been understood, I am sure, by all of the advocates in this appeal. Ground 4, briefly. Do all crimes against humanity require a discriminatory intent? Article 5 makes no mention of it. The Court, this Court, is, in reality, a beast of statute. It has been established by the Security Council of the United Nations. It deprives all of its jurisdiction and all of its power from that source. It has no independent existence. The inclusion of the requirement in the Statute of the Rwanda Tribunal does not indicate, in our submission, that there was no intention to apply the requirement in the former Yugoslavia. The Rwanda Tribunal Statute is supportive of the view that the Security Council does intend to embrace the requirement for discriminatory intent when considering crimes against humanity. The fact of its inclusion in that Statute is no more an advantage to the Prosecution than, in our submission, it is to the Defence. The fact is that Article 5 is silent on the matter, but you have the Secretary-General's report and three interpretative declarations. What status do they have? In our submission, they make it clear that the United Nations intend, as an element of the crime, discriminatory intent. Indeed, I don't think it is suggested that the Secretary-General's report and the three interpretative declarations could be interpreted in any other way. What I think is being suggested is that the Court ought to close its eyes to the assistance that those documents and declarations provide and adopt a blinkered approach to the interpretation of the Statute by confining itself to the actual words of Article 5 and to conclude from that that the absence of the words that are to be found in the Statute of the Rwanda Tribunal is decisive of the point and that no further inquiry is necessary. In our submission, it is not only perfectly permissible to look at the guidance of the Secretary-General's report and the three interpretative decisions, the Appeals Chamber ought to have recourse to those reports and decisions in order to see what mischief the United Nations had in mind when establishing the Statute that brought into existence this court. I appreciate that there is no direct authority in relation to the interpretation of multi-national statutes of this type. However, in national jurisdictions where the interpretation of statutes is more common, one can find an increasing willingness to look at the record of the legislators in order to see what the legislature intended by a statute. Under the English common law, The House of Lords, in the decision of Pepper v. Hart, have said that in the case of any uncertainty or ambiguity, then the Court can have recourse to the transcripts of Parliament, called Hansard, in order to determine what Parliament intended when it passed an Act of Parliament. Such an approach is a sensible and realistic approach in the modern age to the interpretation of statutes. It would, in our submission, be absurd for this Appeals Chamber, in seeking to resolve the full impact and effect of Article 5, to close its eyes to the clearest indication of what the United Nations actually intended. It would be like adopting the approach of Admiral Nelson at the Battle of Trafalgar by putting the telescope to your blind eye. We would encourage you to keep both eyes open to receive all the information that is legitimately available, and I don't think it is suggested that if you do that, then the information contained in the report and decisions clearly indicates that the legislature, the United Nations, clearly intends that there should be a requirement for discriminatory intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, would you take some questions from my colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, how would you react to the proposition whereby the statements in the Security Council by France, the U.S., and the Russian delegates could be equated with preparatory work in a treaty, could be treated as similar to the preparatory work when a treaty is drafted and agreed upon, with the consequence that, as you know, if the text of the treaty is clear, no need exists to resort to preparatory work; the consequence being that, of course, the actual text, the literal text of Article 5, would prevail over those three declarations made by those three representatives in the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: In my submission, Article 5 is not clear because it is silent on the topic, and one can't treat silence as ... Article 5, as drafted, is completely silent upon whether there is or is not a requirement for discriminatory intent. Obviously, if it were to say there is no requirement for discriminatory intent, then the Statute would be clear and I couldn't advance the proposition that I do. In our submission, the absence of any indication either way creates uncertainty as to what the drafters of the treaty actually intended, and it is because of the existence of the uncertainty that you are entitled to look at the preparatory work. In our submission, the fact that it was, in fact, inserted in the Statute for the Rwanda Tribunal only increases the uncertainty as to what was intended in this treaty which, of course, was first in time. If uncertainty does exist, then you can look at the preparatory work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Why do you feel that there is some uncertainty? Actually, Article 5 does not include any requirement concerning discriminatory intent, and you know the Latin maxim, which I will express in my Italian Latin, "ubi lex non distinguit, nec nos distinguere debemus," wherever the law does not make any distinction, the interpreter is not allowed to make similar distinctions. First of all, Article 5 simply does not address the issue of whether or not discriminatory intent is required, and, of course, by implication, that means that such an intent is not required. Then, as for the Statute of the Rwanda Tribunal, of course, Mr. Fenrick I think yesterday pointed out that you can resort to argumentum a contrario, a contrary argument, since there the idea is spelled out, whereas the idea is not to be found in Article 5 of our Statute. The logical conclusion to be drawn is that Article 5 does not intend to embrace or to cover or to include such intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I can obviously see the force of that submission. I am not suggesting Article 5 is ambiguous. It is not. It is perfectly clear. I am suggesting that it creates an uncertainty by its silence, and it is equally consistent with the insertion of the provision in the Rwanda treaty, that the draftsmen, in the light of questions as to whether or not it was a necessary ingredient under this treaty, thought they had better make it absolutely clear once and for all. I can't do any more than put the matter in that way. It is not clear, in our submission, under international law, whether discriminatory intent is a requirement or not. International law, like all areas of law, will evolve and develop in time, and this is an area that has been evolving and developing in recent years. In our submission, although there is no ambiguity here, if silence does create uncertainty as to what the legislation intended, then you are entitled to look at preparatory work. If you came to the conclusion there is no uncertainty at all and it is absolutely clear, then I concede, I've lost. You can't have recourse to it. But in our submission, the court, because it is a creature of statute and one statute, must be alert to the fact that it doesn't have the advantage of a history of appellate decisions to draw upon in forming the guidance for the Trial Chambers in approaching the work that they have to do. The Appeals Chamber, and indeed the court, the trial court in the Tadic case, to an extent are coming to the whole concept of the Tribunal cold, with no precedent, and in our submission, in a situation like that, one should be more ready to look at the preparatory documents in order to be confident that the Tribunal was putting into effect the intention of the legislation than you would in a domestic jurisdiction where the legislation will inevitably have had a history of previous legislation and one can look back through how previous legislation was interpreted and how that has been applied by the courts, and the draftsmen, of course, in drafting legislation in a domestic field, would have known how earlier legislation was interpreted, they would have known how the courts had considered it. Here the draftsmen are coming to it completely cold and the Court is coming to it completely cold, and in those circumstances, one ought to take a more relaxed view at seeking to obtain guidance from this material which you perhaps would not do in a domestic jurisdiction because you would have help from other sources as would the legislators and the draftsmen in creating the treaty in the first place. A slightly circular argument but, of course, the fact that the Trial Chamber thought that it was a requirement and the Prosecution think that it isn't at least demonstrates uncertainty in some minds as to what was intended by the legislation. But there is a certain circularity to that argument that I appreciate. I don't think that I can really advance that submission any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg --

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Can I move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Before you move, I have to say that my mind was exercised by the same issues opened by my brother Judge Cassese. I think I should say that I have, as it were, a philosophical problem about the position which you have put forward to the effect that the language of Article 5 is clear, there is no ambiguity; nevertheless, you feel that the silence, a certain silence in Article 5, creates uncertainty. Isn't that another way of saying there is ambiguity?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I was using the word "ambiguity" to describe the situation where the words of the Statute themselves are unclear and are capable of two different interpretations. Here the Statute is completely silent, and it is that situation that I suggest creates uncertainty. So I was using the words in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Why do you say Article 5 is silent, a point on which my colleague asked you some questions? Isn't the position this, that a draftsman drafts on the basis that the words he uses are going to be interpreted in accordance with the law as the law stands? Now, there seems to be no difficulty about this, that received customary international law at this time distinguishes between two branches of crimes against humanity: (1) the murder-type crimes; (2) the persecution-type crimes. Discrimination is required in relation to the latter but not the former. Wouldn't the draftsman have intended that the words he used in Article 5 would be accordingly construed? If that is so, is there any silence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Well, again, I can see the force of what Your Honour says. All I can say by way of response is that the article does not expressly aver to the need or otherwise of a requirement for discriminatory intent. It is, in fact, silent in the sense that it doesn't expressly say one way or the other. I, of course, accept the force of what Your Honour says, namely, well, there's no need to say it because if you don't say it, everybody knows the answer, which is, I think, the effect of what Your Honour has just posed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me explain to you. Words indicative of a specific requirement will be used only where the draftsman intends to vary from the received meaning of the words he uses. Take the reference to armed conflict. He deliberately inserted in Article 5 a reference to armed conflict because he wished to make it clear that the jurisdiction of the Tribunal was to be accordingly limited in that way, which limitation is not apparent on the basis of received customary international law. When he came to drafting the Rwanda Statute, he omitted those words, whereupon the language used in the case of Rwanda would fall to be received in accordance with the meaning to be ascribed to them by customary international law. Isn't that the position? Additional words, an additional requirement are introduced by the draftsman only where he intends to vary from the meaning which his words would have under received law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Well, I must accept that that is the perceived wisdom of statutory interpretation, and it would be quite absurd for me to suggest otherwise. Of course, I must accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me take you back to a second branch of your interesting submissions on this matter, and this concerns the three declaratory statements. Are you inviting the Court to say that those statements are themselves clear or is there an ambiguity in those statements themselves? Take the Russian statement; this is what it says: "While believing that the text of this Statute addresses the tasks that face the Tribunal and for that reason supporting it, we deem it appropriate to note that according to our understanding, Article 5 of the Statute encompasses criminal acts committed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia during an armed conflict, acts which were widespread or systematic, were aimed against the civilian population, and were motivated by that population's national, political, ethnic, religious, or other affiliation." If you focus on the word "encompasses," all that he's saying there is that, as a matter of fact, murder-type offences may be offences which are, in fact, motivated in these ways. He didn't say that that kind of motivation is essential to all kinds of murder-type offences. The word he used was "encompasses."

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I accept that. The way that we would put the matter is that if the Appeals Chamber were persuaded to look at the Secretary-General's report and the interpretative declarations, then they should all be read together. We would invite the Court to conclude that if read together, they make clear that such an intention was intended. But I do accept that when analysed individually that some of them are less clear than others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let's go back to the Secretary-General's report. Again, how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you mind if I interrupt just at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: My colleague would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to the statement by one of the three representatives, which is by far the most exhaustive and clear, the one by Mrs. Albright as the U.S. representative. She said: "We understand that other members of the Security Council share a view regarding the following clarifications related to the Statute," and then there are various sentences about other provisions. Then she comes to Article 5: "It is understood that Article 5 applies to all acts listed in that article when committed contrary to law during a period of armed conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia as part of a widespread or systematic attack against any civilian population on national, political, ethnic, racial, gender, or religious grounds." So this statement is clearly different from the statement of the Russian representative where you find the ambiguous word "encompasses." How would you comment on this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I prefer Madeleine Albright's statement to that of the Russian delegate but, in our submission, they must be read together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Which one would prevail then? Because, clearly, they are totally different. Madeleine Albright said, "This is our view," the U.S.'s view, "and the view of the other members of the Security Council, and we take it that Article 5 only covers crimes against humanity committed on national, political, ethnic grounds," whereas the Russian representative, according to a possible interpretation, was more flexible. How would you reconcile the two statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Well, they can't be reconciled because they are different. How do you approach the differences between the two? One could say that if the Russian delegate intended that the discriminatory element that we say in truth exists did not exist, then there was no point in him saying anything about it at all. Because if it embraced all crimes, irrespective of discriminatory intent, there's no need for him to say a word about it. The very fact that he's addressed it, unfortunately for me, using the word "encompass" rather than a more restrictive word, the very fact that he addresses the question at all indicates the fact that discriminatory intent was clearly in his mind when he spoke. There is greater clarity to be found, we would say, in the words of Madeleine Albright.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful to my brother Judge Cassese for his question. May I ask you this: Take Madam Albright's statement. Of course, one supposition is that it is exhaustive. It requires discrimination in all cases. But could there be an argument that it is not exhaustive; it is only saying what is factually obvious, that there can be some murder-type offences which are, in fact, based on discriminatory grounds? Would that mean that she was saying that it applies only where there are discriminatory grounds? All she says was that it applies to all acts listed in the article. Did she say it applies only to those acts when discriminatory grounds can be established? Do you think such a contention could be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Well, she certainly didn't say that it could only, but she didn't say that it applied to anything else either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, she didn't. Therefore, my brother is right; there's an ambiguity in the statements. All I'm saying is that leaving aside the apparent conflict between her statement and the Russian statement, I'm not so sure that it cannot be contended that there is an ambiguity even in her own statement. Let's go to the Secretary-General's report. He used the words, I think -- you see it in paragraph 48 of his report, and he says there: "Crimes against humanity refer to inhumane acts of a very serious nature such as wilful killing, torture, or rape, et cetera." Now mark the words "such as." Would you say that he was merely instancing the possibility that some murder-type offences might, in fact, be committed on discriminatory grounds without going on to say that what was intended were only offences which were based on discriminatory grounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It depends how you read it. I mean, I must confess until -- you've asked me to address it. I would have said that the qualification was limited to the list of offences such as wilful killing, torture, rape, but the "such as" was giving illustrations of the crimes, not the discriminatory intent and reflected the fact that it didn't go on to include imprisonment, deportation, enslavement, and extermination, the other crimes under the article. I would submit that on the ordinary reading of that, the qualification does not relate to discriminatory intent but it was a reference to "such as" and selecting three crimes from the list in the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that the text of the Secretary-General's report and of the three statements are so absolutely clear and free of ambiguity as to require the Court to move away from the meaning which received international law would attribute to the text of Article 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I would submit that they were clear enough when viewed collectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: May I move finally, so far as I'm concerned, to ground 2? Thereafter, Mr. Livingston will address the Court on ground 5. I draw initial comfort from the fact that this is now a unanimous decision of the Trial Chamber; Judge McDonald is back with the majority of the Court. There is, in our submission, a distinction between this and the appellate's third ground of appeal. Insofar as the assessment of the evidence in relation to that ground and the witness Nihad Seferovic, we are submitting to the Court that the Trial Chamber didn't have the relevant information contained in the document referred to as Defence Exhibit 14 before them when they made their decision, and the absence of a translated version of that document led them into error that, we submit, this Court could not be satisfied they would have made had they had that document. The position is quite different in relation to ground 2. It is not suggested that the Court didn't pay regard to all the evidence that there was before it. It is submitted on two bases that they came to the wrong conclusion. The first basis, when analysed, in our submission, proceeds on what, on reflection, is an extraordinary proposition. It, when analysed, seems to depend upon the proposition that the three Judges of the distinction and experience of those sitting in the Trial Chamber in this case did not know what was meant by "reasonable doubt" and were unable to apply the test correctly to the facts of this case. We invite the Appeals Chamber to reject the proposition that the Trial Chamber didn't know what is meant by the words "reasonable doubt" and to proceed confidently on the basis that you could be satisfied that they fully understood what those words mean. Furthermore, we would invite the Court to conclude that they applied the correct principles to the facts of the case. It is perfectly true that in paragraph 373 of the judgement reference was made, I think, to the words "bare possibility." Those words, "the bare possibility," viewed in isolation may be curious words for a Trial Chamber to use, but the paragraph which contains those words begins with the words, "This Trial Chamber is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt," and immediately before the reference to "bare possibility," the judgement reads, "However, this Trial Chamber cannot, on the evidence before it, be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had any part in the killing of the five men or any of them." Immediately after the use of the words "the bare possibility," the Court used these words: "It is accordingly a distinct possibility that it may have been the act of a quite distinct group of armed men or the unauthorised and unforeseen act of one of the force that entered Sivci for which the accused cannot be held responsible that caused their deaths." At three points in the same paragraph where the word "bare" was used before the word "possibility," there is, in our submission, a correct expression of the appropriate standard of proof required by the Appeals Chamber. In our submission, in a judgement that extends to hundreds of pages, individual words in the judgement ought not to be subject to the same scrutiny as a Jesuit scholar would apply when interpreting an ancient manuscript. One must look at not just the whole of the paragraph but the whole of the judgement in order to ask oneself, can it be tenably contended that this Trial Chamber didn't know what a reasonable doubt meant? In our submission, it is absolutely clear that they fully understood what those words meant and that they applied them to the facts as they found them. The use of the word "bare" before the word "possibility" in one paragraph that twice refers to the correct standard of proof and then uses the word "distinct" before the same word "possibility" four lines further on ought not to be the basis for overturning a verdict of acquittal and convicting this appellant of effectively the five murders -- not charged as counts of murder, I appreciate, but that's the effect of it -- the five killings that were the subject of this part of the judgement. The facts, in our submission, are entirely consistent with the interpretation of the unanimous Trial Chamber. Here no one witnessed the killings. No one knew who was physically present at that particular spot when the men were killed or any of them. No one was able to confirm or deny that the murderer or murderers was or was not with the group earlier in the other village, Sivci. No witness was able to confirm that the same men who arrived were the same men that left without addition or subtraction. In the absence of such evidence, it is a perfectly reasonable conclusion for the Trial Chamber to come to for them not to be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the group remained intact. They had the advantage of hearing from the witnesses who were actually in the village, and they heard the limited opportunities that they had to view events that were happening in the village from the windows and other places that allowed them, of necessity, a very restricted view of events that day. Furthermore, we submit, the Appeals Chamber has correctly applied the principles of joint enterprise. The conclusion that they made was that the killings may have been the unauthorised and unforeseen act of one of the force that entered Sivci for which the accused cannot be held responsible that caused their deaths. In applying the principle of joint enterprise, the Trial Chamber set out a statement of the law -- one moment. I am afraid I have the wrong reference. It's at page 260. The Trial Chamber, in our view, correctly sets out there and in the paragraphs that flow, up to page 268, an analysis of the law of joint enterprise that is accurate and which, as I understand it, is not the subject of criticism. The Trial Chamber correctly came to the conclusion that in order to be criminally culpable on the principles of joint enterprise, then the person accused must have joined a criminal agreement which he knew at the time could have had the consequences of killing. The Trial Chamber heard the evidence and they concluded that they could not be so satisfied so far as this action was concerned, and they were entitled, in coming to that conclusion, to take account of the fact that in the far larger action at the village of Sivci [real-time transcript read "Jaskici" in error], the action had not involved any killing at all, and the Trial Chamber were quite entitled to conclude that the Prosecution had not been able to discharge the burden on them to prove that on that day the appellant had joined a criminal enterprise which he knew might result in the consequences of killing as opposed to the forcible removal of people to camps. In our submission, the submissions of the Prosecution fell into error so far as the consideration of this aspect of the law is concerned. The proposition advanced was that "We have intent" -- I am looking at page 179 of the transcript, line 4: "We have intent, we have participation, and now in Jaskici itself with this small group of men, we have participation in a common criminal enterprise. This common criminal enterprise was not an unforeseen or an unauthorised enterprise because the enterprise in Jaskici was the same as the enterprise in Sivci, was the same as the enterprise throughout all of opstina Prijedor, and that enterprise was to rid opstina Prijedor of non-Serbs, to rid them of all or at least most of the non-Serbs in that area and to do it by a variety of means, including killings." In our submission, that is not the correct approach. The correct approach is the approach adopted by the Trial Chamber who addressed this question: Has it been proved that this defendant, or appellant as he is now, on that day joined a joint enterprise that he knew that day may have the consequence of killing? It is not enough to say that there may have been some other enterprise involving other people on a wider scale that did embrace in others an appreciation that killing would be caused, it must, before he can be found guilty, be proved that he personally also embraced that knowledge, and that is something that the Trial Chamber, on the facts of this day, could not be satisfied of on the evidence that was presented. The position is that his individual state of mind and his individual knowledge needs to be proved, and it is that which, on the facts of this case, the Prosecution, in the judgement of the Trial Chamber, were unable to do. So on both of the bases advanced, in our submission, the Trial Chamber came to the correct conclusion in acquitting the appellant of responsibility for the deaths of those five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: My colleague wishes to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you through, Mr. Clegg?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The question with regards to the notion of common criminal enterprise, I understand the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor have propounded this notion, within the ambit of it, with reference to Article 7(1). Now, as you know, Article 7(1) of our Statute enumerates five categories: planning, instigating, ordering, committing, or aiding and abetting. So in your view, the notion of common criminal enterprise, under what category does the notion of common criminal enterprise fall: commission or aiding and abetting? Because I understand in some books I read on British criminal law, sometimes the notion of common criminal enterprise is also dealt with in combination with the notion of aiding and abetting, so what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It does embrace aiding and abetting. It can also involve commission as well. But I am using it in the aiding and abetting sense, and you can only aid and abet a criminal enterprise if you know and foresee the possible consequences. So under the English criminal law -- you need, of course, to have a mental element as well. Obviously, you are not guilty of a criminal enterprise if you drive somebody, perfectly innocently, to a site and they kill somebody. It doesn't make you guilty of murder if you merely happen to be the taxi driver who took him there. But if you took him there knowing that he was going to kill, then you would be aiding and abetting the killing by driving him to the scene knowing that he was there and taking his weapon and he to the scene so that he could commit the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But you don't rule out the possibility of this notion coming only within the purview of commission, perpetration, regardless of any aiding and abetting, leaving aside, simply as a sub-category of perpetration?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You think it is only aiding and abetting -- sorry, you don't rule out, you don't exclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I don't exclude it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: That concludes my submissions. Mr. Livingston will now address the Court on ground 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Clegg. The notation supplied to me by the secretariat indicates that you have spent two hours, a little more than two hours, but the Bench acknowledges that the excess has been attributable to questions from the Bench, and so we would be disposed to hear Mr. Livingston ... Would it be all right, Mr. Livingston, if we allocated to you half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just say, I was going to start by making an application for extra time for good behaviour, which is a somewhat unusual request, but certainly everybody so far has kept more than within the schedule, and I think, frankly, we are about two days ahead of where we originally expected to be on Monday morning. So I hope that there is no serious problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. Livingston. You have half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just, before I start, it may be convenient just to mention one possibly quite serious transcription error which may arise out of Mr. Clegg's pronunciation of the village Sivci, because it came out, on the transcript that I saw, as Jaskici, which is, of course, the other village completely, and it must be missed since, of course, Jaskici is an actual place. It was page 56, line 20, if that assists, of today's transcript, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is correct. Please proceed. Would you like to open for a few minutes? I think we have 15 minutes more. You could usefully employ that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, let me start by going to what I hope is the heart of the matter and also start by taking up something which I hope is agreed between the parties, and that is the very simple point that, rightly or wrongly, and it was decided a long time ago, the Tribunal adopted an adversarial system, and whatever elements of the civil law have been imported into it along the way, it is still, in essence, an adversarial system, and that is crucial in the context of this issue of disclosure of Defence witness statements, and it is really perhaps dealt with by the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of Stinchcombe which His Honour Judge Stephen was referred to and in the passage which he referred to. All a defendant is required to do in an adversarial system, and it may be unattractive to some, but this is all he is required to do, is to adopt an adversarial role. Judges in England, and I'm sure in every other adversarial jurisdiction, regularly tell juries -- and for present purposes, I don't think there is any distinction between a court of judges and a jury -- that the prosecution bring the case, the onus of proving it is on them and of proving it beyond reasonable doubt is on them. The defendant doesn't have to prove his innocence; indeed, he doesn't have to prove anything. In my submission, it is an easy step from there, from acknowledging that the defendant doesn't have to prove anything, he can say silent, if he wants, for him to say, and I put the question, of course, rhetorically, "Why should I help the Prosecution?" It is an adversarial system. And one cannot get away from the fact that requiring the Defence to disclose witness statements will help the Prosecution. I can't argue with that because it gives them a statement and it gives them the basis to cross-examine that witness on the basis of what might be a prior inconsistency. So it certainly helps the Prosecution. And the defendant would say, "Look, this is a gladiatorial contest. Why should I help my opponent?" In no other adversarial sort of contest is one opponent required to help the other. So in my submission, the starting point is that the very nature of the adversarial process is actually repugnant to the idea the Defence should be required to disclose their hand to help the Prosecution. It is contrary to the whole concept of the adversarial role. In various adversarial situations, one can have a situation where one adversary is clearly stronger than the other, and again, the whole idea of adversarial contests, whether it is in the legal context or in a sporting context, is to have a fair and even contest insofar as one can. One sees it -- perhaps I can use an analogy which won't be perceived as frivolous -- but if you look at the sport of horse racing on the flat, as it is operated in most Western European countries and in America, if you have horses of one age generation racing against horses from another older generation, the common system is to have a weight-for-age allowance because the older horses are stronger, more experienced, more physically developed, and the idea is that one should equalise their chances, the younger horse with the older one. So it is here that there is an undoubted inequality of arms between Prosecution and Defence, and I do accept the point that Ms. Hollis makes that the inequality is not the same as one sees in a national jurisdiction because, most obviously, the Prosecution does not have the assistance of a national police force. But it is, frankly, naive to plead that the Prosecution does not have great advantages in this jurisdiction as well. The Tribunal has acknowledged it, and just to name but two provisions in -- Article 21 is all about giving a defendant a right in equal terms -- I will come back to that in a minute -- and there is Rule 68 which is the Rule which requires the Prosecution to disclose any evidence of an exculpatory nature which they come across in the course of their investigations. Those are implicit acknowledgements by the draftsmen of the Statute and the Rules that there is an inequality, and of course there is, because they have much, much greater financial resources, and partly as a consequence of that, they can afford to use many investigators in many different countries to gather their evidence. That is not available to the Defence. The other inequality which, of course, is perhaps more particular to this case but it may be more wide-ranging as the jurisdiction of this Tribunal progresses, is, of course, the point that the Trial Chamber raise briefly in paragraph 530, I think it is, of the judgement, that the witnesses called by the Prosecution -- I think I am right in saying -- came exclusively from countries outside Bosnia. If that is wrong, it is only a minimal overstatement. The witnesses called by the Defence, such as they were, came almost exclusively from Republika Srpska, and therein lies a significant inequality. One cannot escape this. The Prosecution, I am sure, are quite right in saying that they have had their difficulties with Republika Srpska. I am not going to deny that because I think it is a well-known fact in this Tribunal that Republika Srpska has proved a recalcitrant state which has not given a great deal of cooperation to anybody in this Tribunal, but it inevitably affects the defendant more than it affects the Prosecution because they don't need witnesses, they didn't need witnesses from Republika Srpska, they could get them from elsewhere, from safe Western European and United States abodes. So the disparity did not affect them anything like as much. Let me turn to the specific provision I mentioned earlier because Ms. Hollis closed, really, her remarks yesterday by saying to you, "Well, look, the matter is dealt with in the Statute. Look at Article 21." I'm not sure if I saw a hint of a blush as she said that because the reality is that that is not what Article 21 is designed to do. Article 21 is designed to give a defendant rights; it is not designed to give the Prosecution any rights at all. It is an acknowledgement that a defendant, as I have indicated already, is not on an equal footing with the Prosecution, and his position requires to be equalised, so he is given these express rights. It is not a question of saying, "Well, the Prosecution's position should be equalised with that of the Defence"; it is a matter of trying to equalise the Defence's position with that of the Prosecution. So in my submission, it is contrary to the whole spirit of that provision for Ms. Hollis to invoke it in her favour as something giving her a right. It is plainly not designed at all to give her any rights whatsoever. In my submission, even if one reads Article 21(4) in terms -- and I am looking particularly at (e) because that was the subparagraph that was invoked yesterday -- it says: "(e) to examine, or have examined, the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf ..."
