It doesn't say anything about the cross-examination of those witnesses of his own that attend and are examined on his behalf or the circumstances under which those witnesses should be examined. So it is not even as though this specific problem is covered expressly in Article 21 at all, but the main point, the really significant point is, that is an Article dealing with the rights of the accused, giving him rights, giving him privileges; it is not intended to give the Prosecution anything; and it shouldn't be invoked to give the Prosecution any such right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: This will be a convenient point, Mr. Livingston?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Just before lunch, I was dealing with the inequality of arms aspect of this question concerning the disclosure of Defence witness statements. It was the English writer, George Orwell, who wrote in his book Animal Farm, "All men are equal but some men are more equal than others." In relation to this particular situation, what it comes to is that the Prosecution are more equal than the Defence, and one shouldn't make orders for the defence to disclose witness statements which are likely to have the consequence of increasing the disparity between the parties rather than equalising their respective positions. Let me pass on to the various Rules because that deals, I hope, with the statutory provision in Article 21. The Rule that I think is still relied on, despite Ms. Hollis's very proper concession this morning about the Dokmanovic case, is Rule 54. That's the Rule which says: "At the request of either party or proprio motu, a Judge or a Trial Chamber may issue such orders, summonses, subpoenas, warrants and transfer orders as may be necessary for the purposes of an investigation or for the preparation or conduct of the trial." Now, there are two points that arise out of that as to why that provision should not be used to make the Defence disclose witness statements. The first is this, and it's essentially a point I've made already, that included in that Rule is the word "necessary." In other words, the Trial Chamber should not do any of those things, issue any of the orders or subpoenas or warrants or whatever, unless it is necessary for the purposes of an investigation or for the preparation or conduct of the trial. Now, bearing in mind the adversarial nature of the trial and that the defendant doesn't have to prove his innocence or anything doesn't have to assist the Prosecution -- in other words, it can take up a wholly adversarial role. It cannot, in my submission, be said that it is necessary for the preparation or conduct of the trial that the defendant or his lawyers are made to disclose those documents. It's inherent in the concept of an adversarial system. It's not necessary, so the Rule doesn't apply. In any event, I would submit that that Rule must be looked at in its context. It's the first Rule in a section headed "Orders & Warrants." The other Rules in that section deal with execution of arrest warrants, cooperation of states, procedure after arrest, national extradition proceedings, failure to execute a warrant or transfer order, transmission of arrest warrants, advertisement of indictment, et cetera. They are all matters which are intimately connected with the investigation and to enable the trial to proceed smoothly. You issue warrants for people's arrests. You issue summonses for them to attend court, subpoenas if they are reluctant, transfer orders to get people from another jurisdiction to this jurisdiction. In my submission, the word "orders" should be construed ejusdem generis with those other words, and it would be to strain the language of the Rule to say that the word "orders" should bear no relation to what everything else in the section is dealing with. It might, for example, cover things like orders to protect sensitive information. It might cover orders such as binding orders which are, of course, invoked to assist investigation and preparation. But in my submission, it's stretching the language of the Rule in its context and where it lies within the Rules to say that it covers something like disclosure by the Defence of witness statements. I'm fortified in that view by the fact that, of course, the issues arising out of disclosure are dealt with specifically later in the Rules, particularly of importance, Rules 66 and 67. It's Rule 66 which obliges the Prosecution to supply copies of statements of witnesses, so that is specifically dealt with. That is their obligation, as well as, of course, the indictment and supporting material. No obligation is specified for the Defence to do anything. Following the googly, if I may use a cricketing metaphor, that His Honour Judge Cassese bowled at Mr. Clegg earlier this morning about silence, there is significant silence here about Defence witness statements. There is no order there or no obligation, and it's quite clear, there is no ambiguity, however you interpret that word, no uncertainty, no obligation to disclose witness statements in that Rule or, indeed, in any other Rule in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It goes even further than that because Rule 67, which is dealing specifically with reciprocal disclosure, one might think, would set out, comprehensively, exactly what the Defence have to disclose, and it's confined to matters in Rule 67(A)(ii), defence of alibi and, secondly, any special defence like diminished or lack of mental responsibility. Those are the two things that the Defence must notify the Prosecutor of. Nothing else is mentioned. Silence, unambiguous silence. In my submission, one shouldn't try and fill that gap with something that isn't there. The other Rule, of course, which perhaps I can just mention in passing, I don't think there's a great deal of dispute between Prosecution and Defence on this, is Rule 70, which, of course, is what Judge McDonald relied upon. I think the Prosecution and Defence are at one, that with the greatest respect to her, she's wrong about the applicability of that Rule because she was of the view that -- we're looking at capital A, it says: "Notwithstanding the provisions of Rules of 66 and 67, reports, memoranda, or other internal documents prepared by a party, its assistants or representatives ... are not subject to disclosure or notification under the Rules." She thought that that covered witness statements but, of course, the problem with that would be that it would be in flagrant contradiction, as far as the Prosecution are concerned, with the express words of Rule 66. On the basis that what is source for the goose is source for the gander, one shouldn't say that witness statements are covered for the Defence in Rule 70 but not the Prosecution. It's got to be consistent. In my submission, it is an error, with the greatest respect to the learned Judge, to have thought that the words in Rule 70 could cover witness statements by either party. I pass on to Rule 89 which, of course, is much discussed by Judge Stephen, and I think I can adopt respectfully what he says about that, but in essence, what one's looking at here is Rule 89(B) which says that: "In cases not otherwise provided for in this Section, a Chamber shall apply rules of evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and a consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law." Now, I've already made the submission and, I think, as clearly as I can that the spirit of the Statute, and it's Article 21 that seems to be the relevant one as far as the Prosecution are concerned, the spirit of the Statute is against the disclosure by the Defence of witness statements. The question is about general principles of law, and again, I would respectfully suggest that what Judge Stephen said about that is almost common sense, that where one is dealing with an adversarial system of justice, as we are here, that you shouldn't go and look at the general principles of law in some other type of system with some other basis which might explain why it develops different rules of evidence and procedure. One should, in my submission, find highly persuasive, as Judge Stephen states, the practice, the general practice in countries which adopt an adversarial system. Again, I say this with the greatest respect to the American lawyers in the court, so I don't mean any disrespect to them at all, because every lawyer, I suspect, tends to think that his own country's system is the best, but it seems that on this issue and according to the research as done by counsel and, indeed, by the Judges of the Trial Chamber, it seems that the American system, based on the case of the United States v. Nobels is frankly unique amongst adversarial systems in making provision, in fact, in imposing an obligation on the Defence to disclose witness statements. In my submission, one cannot interpret the phrase "general principles of law" from the practice in one jurisdiction amongst the quite numerous which adopt this type of system of justice. In my submission, one should be looking to see what the general practice is of all the countries which adopt this type of system. In my submission, it's quite clear, as Judge Stephen makes obvious in his opinion, what it perhaps boils down to at the end of the day is this issue of privilege. You have the documentary material or at least some of it which Judge Stephen refers to in the bundle of authorities which the Defence or the appellant has submitted. In particular, it's divider 14 where I've extracted various pages from Cross and Tapper on Evidence. I would, first of all, refer you to page 484 which refers to the case of Anderson v. The Bank of British Columbia. It's an old case basically saying that you have no right to see your adversary's brief, and if you have no right to see that, then you can't see the materials in his brief either. That's an old case. As Tapper points out, things have moved on, things have changed, but it's quite apparent if you read the rest of the section on a legal advisor's work in Cross and Tapper on Evidence, one thing that comes out is that there's no change to the principle that communications between a legal advisor and third parties are privileged where there is a definite prospect of litigation in contemplation by the client. So whatever the position might be in other circumstances, that is the rule that applies here, manifestly so, because the issue arose in connection with the witness statement of Witness W, as he was known. That was a witness statement that had been obtained after Mr. Tadic had been indicted and, indeed, I think after he had been transferred to this court. But in any event, it could not possibly be said that criminal prosecution against him was not clearly about to happen. So the circumstances in which that witness statement was taken were very definitely in the contemplation of litigation, and if one reads what the editor of Cross and Tapper says, it is quite apparent that whatever other radical changes there may have been since the early case of Anderson v. The Bank of British Columbia, that rule has not changed, and in my submission, the Defence witness statements for those reasons are quite clearly, on the practice which is summarised in that book, privileged, and Judge Stephen reviews the various authorities in other jurisdictions, the Australian authorities, Baker v. Campbell, Grant v. Downs, the Canadian authorities, R. v. Peruta, amongst others, R. v. Stinchcombe. He also looks -- well, in fact, he quotes what Mr. Wladimiroff told him, and the Trial Chamber accepted, that neither in the courts of the Netherlands nor in other European courts with which he was familiar could production be obtained by the prosecution of -- statements of Defence witnesses. So even in civil law systems, Mr. Wladimiroff is right, which I expect he is, it wouldn't happen. There is also even a reference to the opinion of Sir Gordon Slynn in the European Court of Justice, again upholding this same principle. So in my submission, the adversarial system points to these type of documents clearly being the subject of privilege, that privilege has not been waived by Mr. Tadic, and the only remaining issue, therefore, is whether it is waived after the witness has given his evidence; in other words, after he has given his evidence in chief, as English lawyers would say, or I think as Americans would say, after his evidence, his direct evidence, before he is cross-examined. Again, I come back to this central point, in closing, which I started with, that to hold that that privilege has been waived would involve again adopting a stance which would be quite contrary to that in an adversarial system, it would be quite contrary to the concept that a defendant is, in an adversarial system, entitled to take up an adversarial role in that system, to say to the Prosecution, "You prove your case. I don't have to help you. You have chosen to prosecute me. You've got the evidence. You prove it." In my submission, not only is there no authority but it is -- again I repeat; I hope not to the infinite boredom of the Court -- repugnant to the idea of the adversarial system that such a privilege should be held to be waived merely because the witness has given his evidence in chief and simply as an aid to the Prosecution to try and demolish him, if they can, with the assistance of a witness statement. So, Your Honour, there it is. The objections to this line of the appeal, the cross-appeal, are: (1) in the adversarial nature of the system; (2) because of the inequality of arms which it would increase, there would be a greater disparity if one allowed it; and (3) because of the issue of privilege which, according to general principles which seem to apply in most adversarial jurisdictions -- in fact, all but one -- would enable these documents to be privileged, and in my submission, remain privileged to the end. Unless there are any other matters that you'd wish me to deal with, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If I may ask you a question or two. You spoke of the question of equality of arms. I understand you to be saying that the principle of equality of arms requires compensation to be given to the Defence for, shall I say, its natural inequalities in gathering evidence. That translates into a principle of a right to silence. He has a right to put the Prosecution to proof of the charge which the Prosecution has brought against him. But if he decides to break his silence by offering proof, should the Court take the position that to evaluate that proof, the Court must apply to the proof the same tests, the same machinery, as it would apply to the proof advanced by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm afraid I can't really answer that question in any other way than I already have, and I don't wish to repeat myself, but in my submission, to require him to do that would be contrary to the nature of his adversarial role in the trial. I appreciate that in some ways it can be said, yes, it would be very nice to be able to evaluate statements, it may well be -- the Prosecution would love it because they would be able to at least carry out some check on what the witness has said, but that's not the way the adversarial system works and it is not in keeping with the adversarial concept that the defendant should offer that help. He can give evidence on his own account or put forward evidence to protect himself to put forward his defence, but he is not obliged to offer any further assistance. In fact, there is, in my submission, a distinction between putting forward evidence to defend himself and actually offering assistance, which is what the requirement, that he disclose witness statements, would do. I hope that answers the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. I will take due note of what you have said. You accept that the common law system has been evolving and has been evolving in different directions in different law areas within the common law system. Does that, do you think, present the Tribunal, the Appeals Chamber, with a problem of selection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Well, I think that may depend on the particular issue of the common law that you are dealing with. It is, with respect, quite a wide question, but applying -- I'll try to answer the question as it is plainly intended in relation to this issue. I hope my references to Cross and Tapper are perhaps helpful, being much more learned in the law than I am, but the editor, the current editor, reviews the way the privilege issue has developed since the Anderson case, which is -- I am just looking for the date of it, it's a very early case -- 1876, and he points out how matters have changed radically; but whatever else has changed in the field of privilege, and maybe, at the end of the day, it boils down to that, the one thing that has not changed is that privilege can be claimed for communications with the client or, indeed, third parties when litigation is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You refer to Rule 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That deals with the subject of supplying to the Defence advance copies of witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Am I right that what is involved here is a claim by the Prosecution to see a Defence witness statement after the witness has given his evidence in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Well, I think that's the very least they would ask for. I think, frankly, they would probably like to have it pre-trial, if they possibly could. The answer to your question, I suppose, is "Yes," that is the Prosecution contention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That, in fact, is what they are asking for. Whatever else, whatever larger request they might have had in mind, that is, in fact, what they are asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is now -- I think it is now conceded that the Dokmanovic situation is rather different. I think that was pre-trial. Ms. Hollis would probably know that better than me. But, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If you ignore the question of privilege, what is there to stop counsel, when cross-examining a witness, from asking the witness if the witness had made a previous statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Well, let me say, first of all, I think it is rather difficult just to shut away the area of privilege because if a prosecuting advocate did that in my country or, indeed, I suspect, most others, his opponent would immediately jump up and say, "That is privileged information. You can't have it." That would be the objection which would be raised because that's the first thing that comes to mind. Leaving aside the issue of privilege, I think the only other answers I can give are those which I have referred to already in the other two arguments: (1) that it is contrary to this concept of the adversarial system and the adversarial role that somebody is being required to assist the Prosecution or the Court in some other way than simply giving his evidence and being cross-examined on what he says and volunteers himself; and (2) because, in my submission, it does offend against this principle of equality of arms which, while different in its nature from that which would normally arise in a national court, is still very much there here and should not be forgotten about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On the three categories which you presented, that is, the adversarial system, equality of arms, and privilege, would you care to prioritise them to say which of them you rely on most strongly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I have to say that I think they are all very strong grounds and I think it would be invidious to pick on them. I have divided it up, really, because this issue is what I might call a basic principles issue, and it is, for that reason, terribly important to the development of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, I appreciate, but I suspect that, answering the question at very short notice, I suspect the answer is probably that privilege is the single most important point. But I would urge the Chamber to accept them all as being, frankly, equally important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you, Mr. Livingston. I also understand the stress which you seem to lay on the third category --

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- if for no other reason than that coincides with my own impressions of the strength of your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I take some comfort from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. That ends the response?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Can I just, with respect, raise one completely different matter in relation to something yesterday? Again, it may be a matter of correction of the record. I hope it is maybe just convenient for me to do it now. You may have noticed in the transcript of yesterday that there was a reference -- and I'm not sure exactly where it was -- but to a mysterious advocate who is not here, Mr. Abell ... Has it? Well, I'm grateful. If it has been altered, so be it, but the Chamber will hear from him clearly next week and not this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That then concludes the response?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So I turn the matter over to Ms. Hollis for a reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it would be easier to take it in reverse order and let me begin our reply and then have Mr. Fenrick complete it. I have very few comments regarding the response to ground 2, Your Honour. First of all, we would suggest that contrary to the appellant's position, individual words are important when these individual words are used to explain why the Trial Chamber believed that the Prosecution's burden had not been met and where the words indicate the standard that the Trial Chamber is using to determine what constituted a reasonable doubt. So in that context, we suggest that the words in the paragraph, paragraph 373, were significant. The Prosecution does agree that the Trial Chamber correctly set out the law relating to joint enterprise. We suggest that they misapplied it, and we suggest that this misapplication is apparent when we consider their findings under paragraph 6 as to Counts 10 and 11 because there the Trial Chamber applied this concept of joint enterprise and found the accused guilty even though, in those facts, they found that earlier, in the events culminating in the sexual mutilation, that the accused, at that time the accused, had actively directly participated in tortures and beatings. They held him criminally liable for that and found him guilty. However, they also found him guilty for acts where he did not directly participate. In fact, the sexual mutilation of Fikret Harambasic, they found that the accused did not directly participate, but that his continued presence rendered him culpable as part of the joint criminal enterprise. We suggest that same interpretation would lead to culpability here in Jaskici. We certainly agree that you must look to the entire judgement in assessing whether the Trial Chamber here correctly applied the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt and you must look to the entire judgement in order to put this idea of joint criminal enterprise in its proper context, and the concept here is that the joint criminal enterprise was much broader than the Trial Chamber envisioned for the counts in question and that indeed this joint criminal enterprise encompassed acts of extreme brutality and killings and that the accused had participated throughout in this joint criminal enterprise of ethnic cleansing and so the accused was proven not just at Jaskici to have a conscious determination to commit acts that deliberately and substantially and directly contributed to the commission of the crimes in Jaskici but that we can show that not just by the facts there but by the other facts of record, the other evidence showing his participation, and that also, because of these other facts, he would have foreseen that this was a possible outcome of this violent behaviour on that date. He certainly would have known it was authorised. Therefore, by his participation, he meets the requirements for joint enterprise liability. That is where we believe that the Trial Chamber misapplied the law. If there are no questions on ground 2, I will move on to ground 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As to ground 5, the appellant has referred to many Rules, including 89(B), which we believe is an appropriate Rule here because there is no Rule that specifically addresses what the Prosecution was requesting. 89(B), you will note, indicates that, first of all, where there is no such Rule, the Trial Chamber should rule in a way that is most consistent with the fair determination of the matter and, secondly, most consistent with the Statute. It is only after that that we get to general principles of law. The Prosecution certainly agrees that there were no existing Rules so that 89(B) would apply. However, in determining what is most consistent with a fair determination of the matter, we suggest you look at the real purpose for the Rule of disclosure of witness statements. It is not to assist either side, it is not to try to create a balance where there was none, it is to assist the triers of fact by allowing the opposing party to bring inconsistencies to the attention of the fact-finder so the fact-finder is fully informed before the fact-finder makes determinations about what evidence is credible and what evidence is not. So that, indeed, the Prosecution request was most consistent with a fair determination of the matter before the Trial Chamber. We further suggest that the Prosecution request was consistent with the Statute, and here we will turn to Article 21, which has been discussed by the appellant, and yesterday there was no blush when the Prosecution referred to Article 21 because indeed the Prosecution very seriously takes the plain language and the plain meaning of the language in that Article, and inherent in that language is equality, and when we look specifically at sub-part 4 and sub-part (e) of sub-part 4, it indicates equality in the sense that the Defence may obtain and examine witnesses under the same conditions as the Prosecution, and it is not fanciful to say that the condition imposed upon the Prosecution is that, for witnesses the Prosecution calls, if statements exist, those statements will be turned over. That is equality and that is what we take the plain word to mean: parity. Not that the Prosecution must but that the Defence need not. That is not an argument of equality, that is an argument of inequality. We have also heard mentioned several times that this submission should be rejected because of this inequality in other areas, for example, the fact that the Prosecution has many more resources. We suggest to you that is totally irrelevant to this issue. But since it has been raised, let's at least, in passing, refer to that argument. The Prosecution has a mandate in this Tribunal that is very expansive. The mandate is to investigate serious violations of international humanitarian law throughout the entire former Yugoslavia and, where sufficient evidence exists, to bring forth indictments and to prosecute. That mandate is much broader than the mandate that an individual accused or Defence counsel has in a case that involves one accused and specific charges. So this argument about resources that the Prosecution has we suggest is a misdirected argument. That position aside, however, Your Honours, of course Defence counsel and the appellant are totally free to come to the registry and to the Trial Chamber and to the Appellate Chamber and request such additional resources as they need to be able to fully carry forth their case, and we believe that has been done, in fact, in the Tadic case. So again, this issue of resources has no impact on ground number 5. If we really look at ground number 5 here, what do we come down to? Now, the appellant has argued to you that an accused has an absolute right to put on no evidence, to remain silent, and to force the Prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and the Prosecution totally accepts that and submits it is totally irrelevant to the issue before you. The issue here has gone well beyond that. The issue here is, where an accused chooses not to remain silent, chooses to present evidence, and that evidence is put forward to the fact-finder for evaluation, the issue here is: Once the appellant decides to put forward evidence, should that evidence be tested? We suggest, yes, indeed, it should. And once an appellant chooses to put forward evidence, what right prevents the testing of that evidence? Is it the right to put on evidence that may not be tested, that must simply be accepted? No such right exists. Is it the right to put on evidence that is contradicted by earlier statements of a witness and to hide that from the Trial Chamber? No such right exists. Is it the right to put on evidence that is, in fact, untruthful and is contradicted and shown to be untruthful by earlier statements? No such right exists. So we are not dealing with deprivation of a right of the accused. What we are dealing with is a way to assist the fact-finder, not the Prosecution, the fact-finder, in carrying out their mandate of determining what is reliable evidence. That is what we are talking about here. It is not barred by the Rules, it is not barred by the Statute, it, in fact, promotes the interests of justice, it promotes the truth-seeking process, but it in no way requires the accused to take that first step and come forward and put on evidence. It only applies once that first step is taken. We suggest that it would promote the mandate of this Tribunal, the interests of justice, the truth-seeking process to indeed rule that once the Defence puts forward a case and puts on witnesses, if there are statements in existence, those statements must be disclosed to the Prosecution so that the witness's evidence can be fully tested. Those are my comments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, Mr. Livingston relied on three categories in making his submission on ground 5. As I understood him, he regarded all three categories as equal but he regarded the third category, if I may say so, as a little more equal than number 1 and number 2; that is, the client-counsel privilege. Have you dealt with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would be happy to make a further response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: There is in this Tribunal, by virtue of the Rules that the Judges of this Tribunal have adopted, there is a very strict attorney-client privilege. It is between the attorney and the client. Defence witnesses are not clients of the attorneys. They are witnesses coming to a court to give evidence. In fact, in some of the trials before this Court, Judges have made statements that all witnesses coming before this Court are not a witness of the party; they are, in fact, a witness of the Court. There has certainly some truth to that. It may not be true in terms of who actually calls the witness and directs them and who can cross-examine them, but in terms of why witnesses are called, that is correct. It is to give evidence to the fact-finders so that the truth may be found. In that regard, we suggest witnesses are not clients of the Defence. In fact, if they were, it could be that there were some conflict of interest that would require the Defence attorney to have to withdraw from that case. They are not witnesses; they are not clients. We believe that the attorney-client privilege, as it is drawn in this Tribunal, is not applicable, and we would urge you not to expand that privilege. We do not believe it is necessary to protect legitimate attorney-client interests. We believe that it would result in protection of information that would be detrimental to the truth-seeking process, such as prior statements from Defence witnesses. If you have not adopted that broader privilege, we would ask that you have not do so, and we would submit that that privilege should not have been used here as a basis for the Trial Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How would you define the client-counsel privilege then? I know it's a broad question, but would you say that the privilege would encompass a previous statement given by the accused himself to his counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our submission would be that to the extent an accused again foregoes his right to remain silent and comes forward and testifies, to the extent he has made prior statements about that same testimony, by coming forward, he has consciously waived any sort of protection he had for those prior statements. If he has made other statements unrelated to his testimony, we would suggest that is protected. We would further suggest that Judges may be even more protective of an accused than they would be of other Defence evidence, and so Judges may be more inclined to perhaps extend more of a protection for an accused who testifies even than for others, because it is the accused who has the absolute right to remain silent and not incriminate himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, we thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I will turn it over to my colleague, Mr. Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now it's Mr. Fenrick. Mr. Fenrick, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we've already used up the 15 minutes that were assigned for rebuttal time. If I might request, say, perhaps a maximum of ten minutes to address specifically ground number 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You would like ten minutes for ground number 1. Are there any other grounds that you will be handling?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I am prepared to speak to the remaining grounds, which are grounds 3 and 4, but I didn't intend to make any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Suppose you gave us a ballpark figure of the total time-span you would require.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: In totality?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: In totality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then you are undercutting us; we were willing to give you 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Ten should do, I believe. In connection with ground 1, which is, of course, concerned with the protected person status under Article 2, as Your Honours will recollect in the various briefs that have been filed, there are three separate tests for attribution, which perhaps might be the most appropriate expression, or the linkage between the accused and a side to the international armed conflict. Two of the tests, the effective control test and the agency test, are rooted in the Nicaragua decision. The third test, the demonstrable link test, which was the one which we had suggested was the most appropriate, is both the lowest standard, the easiest one to reach. Presumably, if one reaches effective control or agency, one has also easily, quite comfortably reached the demonstrable link standard. We submit that there is an adequate legal basis for the demonstrable link or what one might more appropriately call an almost web of different ties between the accused and a side to the conflict test implicit in the Geneva Conventions themselves and in the existing customary law, specifically post-World War II cases involving individual criminal responsibility. It has been suggested by the Defence that the effective control test and the agency test are both ones which are easy to apply and that we are opening the door to a test which is more difficult to apply. It would be our submission that, in fact, all three tests leave ample scope for interpretation. If one might observe, we appear to have had rather substantial differences between various Judges at the Trial Chamber concerning the application of the effective control test. If it was that simple to apply, perhaps we would not have had as much difficulty at the Trial Chamber level as we have had. It is submitted by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, you are referring to the fact that the dissenting Judge considered that on the facts, the control test was satisfied, whereas the majority was of another view?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. It is the submission of the Prosecution that we meet the demonstrable link test. We also meet both of the other tests, if for no other reason than that paragraph 115 of the majority decision, which one might look at almost as the paymaster provision of the judgement, clearly indicates that what we have is the FRY paying its servants on an individual basis, and its servants comprise virtually the entire officer cadre of the VRS. This is not a mere provision for the supply of logistical or financial assistance. A second point which we would like to address is one which has been discussed a bit, and that is the overlap or the relationship between state responsibility and individual criminal responsibility. It would be our submission that state responsibility and individual criminal responsibility are not or do not cover at all times the exact same area. If we start with the earliest provision in Article 3 of Hague Convention IV of 1907, we have a provision: "A belligerent party which violates the provisions of the said regulations shall, if the case demands, be liable to pay compensation. It shall be responsible for all acts committed by persons forming part of its armed forces." At the end of the Second World War, we had a number of war crimes cases concerning individual criminal responsibility which clearly assigned individual criminal responsibility to individuals who would not come within the scope of that Hague Convention provision, who were not members of the armed forces, who may have degrees or relationships of varying tenuousness with one of the belligerents. We then move on to the Geneva Conventions of 1949. It would be our submission that exactly the same structure continued on. We have Article 29 of Geneva Convention IV which certainly talks about the party to the conflict: "In whose hands protected persons may be is responsible for the treatment accorded to them by its agents irrespective of any individual responsibility which may be incurred." It would be our submission that although the party to the conflict may be responsible for the activities of its agents for the purposes of financial compensation, clearly there could be circumstances in which offences occur when a victim is "in the hands of a party" but not -- the fact the offence is not committed by one of its agents. For example, we could have some activity in occupied territory, any range of activity in occupied territory. We could have something occurring in the territory of the high contracting party where the victim is virtually, by definition, in the hands of the high contracting party but the grave breach may be committed by somebody who is not an agent of the high contracting party. It could be committed by a citizen; it could be committed by anybody. Somewhat similarly, if we move along to Additional Protocol I where we have Article 85 -- excuse me. I've managed to tie myself in knots here. Article 85(5) of Additional Protocol I states: "Without prejudice to the application of the conventions and of this protocol, grave breaches of these instruments," meaning also the grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, "shall be regarded as war crimes." So we can't distinguish that on the basis that only war crimes can be committed against a wider range of individuals because here all grave breaches are also war crimes. Then, of course, we have Article 91 of Additional Protocol I, and Additional Protocol I, of course, was applicable in the territory of the former Yugoslavia at the time which is the subject of this indictment. Article 91: "A party to the conflict which violates the provisions of the Convention or of this Protocol shall, if the case demands, be liable to pay compensation. It shall be responsible for all acts committed by persons forming part of its armed forces." There are a range of things for which the state may be responsible, and there has been a range of things for which the state may be responsible, since we have been talking about individual criminal responsibility and the prosecution of war crimes primarily in the post-World War II area, and there is also a range of things for which individuals may be held criminally responsible. They do not necessarily overlap. The last comment which we would like to make in connection with this particular ground of appeal is that the Prosecution, in fact, concedes that there is no burden on the Defence to show -- when we're talking about armed conflict or armed conflicts, there is no burden on the Defence to show that there is a separate internal conflict unrelated to the international conflict. It is up to the Prosecution to establish that what might be viewed as an internal conflict is, in fact, intimately tied to the international conflict. Having said that, it is the submission of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You accept Mr. Clegg's position --

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I accept that part, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- that once an issue has been raised as to whether there was an internal conflict in addition to an international conflict, the burden is on the Prosecution to disprove that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. It is, however, submitted that we have more than amply established the very close relationship between the so-called conflict involving the Republika Srpska and the VRS with Bosnia and the actual overriding conflict between the FRY and Bosnia. These conflicts were one in the same. Those are all the comments that I have in connection with ground number 1, Your Honours. As I said, the other two grounds -- well, if you wish to pose questions concerning either grounds 1, 3, or 4, we are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I've finished. I shall proceed to my seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I will react to that last submission with delight, and congratulations to you for keeping time so well. That concludes the Prosecution's cross-appeal on judgement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then we will turn to the appellant's appeal on sentencing. I know it's a wee bit early, but there seems here to be a natural breakwater in the proceedings, and I wonder whether this might be a time to take our break and to come back exactly in half an hour. If you would like to start now, that's fine. We can start for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I think I'll take the opportunity of the early coffee break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thought so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It's nice to be at one with the Tribunal so consistently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. We will, let us say, resume at ten minutes to the hour; is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It's a little less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: This sitting is resumed. We come now to the third and final branch of the appeal, that is, the appellant's appeal on sentencing. Mr. Clegg, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I am. May it please Your Honours. Turning to the question of the appeal against sentence, on one reading of the Statute of the Tribunal, it could be said that no such appeal can lie because there does not appear to be any express provision for an appeal against sentence in terms. Article 25 that deals with appellant proceedings is couched in the following way: "The Appeals Chamber shall hear appeals from persons convicted by the Trial Chambers or from the Prosecutor on the following grounds: An error on a question of law invalidating a decision or an error of fact which has occasioned a miscarriage of justice." Both of those expressions lie more happily within the concept of an appeal against conviction, but we would submit that there should be a generous and an elastic approach to those words, because the drafters of the Statute could not have intended to have precluded an appeal against sentence where such a sentence was right and proper. It can be argued, in our submission, that an unfair sentence must be a result of an error -- it may be difficult to identify -- or fact by the Trial Chamber because no Trial Chamber would ever want to pass an unfair sentence, and an unfair sentence is itself a miscarriage of justice. It could also be argued in relation to some aspects of the sentence appeal that they do relate to an error on a question of law, and to that extent, if there be an error in relation to the appropriate law as it applies to sentencing, then that is capable, we would submit, of invalidating the decision of sentence, leaving it open to this Appeals Chamber to revise the decision taken by the Trial Chamber which is one of its powers under Article 25(2). We would submit that the word there "revise" embraces the substitution of a fair sentence for an unfair sentence. We would submit that there cannot have been any intention of the drafters to prevent an appeal against sentence. There is, to my knowledge, no jurisdiction that does not have a power to review sentence following conviction, and here, if the sentence is, in the judgement of the Appeals Chamber, unfair, we would invite a generous interpretation of the words of the Statute to enable that unfairness to be remedied. Moving now to the merits of the application, I hope I can encompass the points we raise briefly. First, we submit that a total sentence of 20 years was unfair in that it was longer than the facts of the case required or demanded. The reasons why we say the sentence of 20 years was too long are as follows: First, we submit that particularly in sentencing the very first defendant to have been convicted by a Trial Chamber of crimes in the former Yugoslavia, it was incumbent on the Trial Chamber to have in mind the development of an appropriate tariff of sentences to reflect the varying culpability of different defendants. Such a tariff must inevitably reserve for those most culpable of the highest sentences and reflect in lower sentences those of less culpability. The rank, position of command, activities, and position of power in the region of this appellant were such that ought to have placed him, in the importance of defendants, at the very bottom of the list of culpability. The Trial Chamber here were not dealing with sentencing a decision-maker, somebody who formulated policy, somebody who commanded a body of men; one was dealing with somebody of, on any view, a comparatively lowly status. In our submission, that fact has not been reflected in the pitching of the sentence at 20 years because it does not allow sufficient flexibility to impose an appropriate sentence that would demand a higher tariff against somebody who was much more culpable, a decision-maker, somebody who was formulating policy. That is the first submission that we make, that the Appeals Chamber must have regard to the development of a tariff of sentencing that properly distinguishes levels of culpability and levels of responsibility. Secondly, we would submit that, under Article 24, the Trial Chamber is enjoined to have recourse to the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of former Yugoslavia, Article 24(1). Expert evidence was heard by the Trial Chamber in relation to that issue. I confess, it was not at all times a model of clarity, but doing as best that I can to extract the principle from it, it would appear that in the absence of the death sentence, a sentence of 20 years' imprisonment was the maximum penalty permitted under local law. That factor is a factor that will also be a matter that the Trial Chamber will need to have recourse to when passing sentences on others committed who are, we would say, more culpable and higher in the command structure than this defendant. Third, we would submit that insufficient attention was paid to the personal circumstances of this defendant. First, he, and I expect many others, were subjected to a deliberate propaganda campaign in the area in which they lived which clearly encouraged participation in ethnic cleansing. That, of course, does not excuse criminal responsibility, but it is a factor and helps to explain why a man of previously good character, with no question of any previous offending of any kind, behaved in the way that the Trial Chamber found proved. He is a prisoner who has had to serve and will continue to have to serve his sentence in a foreign state to him; he will be, of necessity, away from his wife and young family during the period that he serves his sentence and will be isolated from others of his own nationality. Indeed, for much of the time that he has already served, he was the only prisoner in the U.N. detention centre and has, in effect, been serving as a remand prisoner in solitary confinement. He will, upon release, suffer from the notoriety of being the first war criminal convicted, and for that and other reasons, return to his native region will probably be impossible. In our submission, those factors combine to demonstrate that the total sentence of 20 years was an unfair sentence in all the circumstances of this case. May I move to two separate points which we submit reflect an error in the application of sentencing policy by the Trial Chamber that would result in injustice unless this Court were to revise the order. The Trial Chamber sought to direct that the appellant serve a minimum sentence of ten years. I cannot find any power for the Trial Chamber to have imposed that minimum period. Of course, nobody can stop a Trial Chamber imposing a recommendation, and any jurisdiction in which a prisoner is serving would, I anticipate, give due weight to any recommendation of the Trial Chamber. So I am not suggesting that they can't give a recommendation. What I submit is manifestly unfair is that they directed that the period of ten years does not begin to run until after the conclusion of the appeal process. The effect of that is to penalise the appellant for exercising his right of appeal. It also has the effect of penalising the appellant for the obstruction of Republika Srpska that has delayed the hearing of this appeal and has the effect of penalising the appellant for the procedural delays that are inevitable in any proceedings of this kind. We submit that that is fundamentally unfair, it imposes a penalty on the right to appeal and is inconsistent with the thrust of the Statute which is designed to give an appellant a right of appeal which ought not to be accompanied by a counterpenalty, and it is, in reality, a penalty because any sentence that is reflected by a minimum recommendation is going to be a sentence that must last, if the recommendation is accepted here, ten years from when that recommendation starts. If it starts today, the appellant will have served 15 years of the 20-year sentence before he could be eligible for release because he has already been in custody some five years. The effect is also, of course, to penalise the appellant for the time taken in preparing the case for trial and penalise him for the difficulties that were occasioned pre-trial, that which we have touched on earlier. We submit that although there is nothing wrong with a minimum recommendation, justice can only be achieved if that minimum recommendation operates from the time the appellant lost his liberty; otherwise, it is to go behind the provision to allow credit for time served whilst unconvicted. So we would invite the Appellate Chamber, in relation to whatever sentence you determine is fair, to make a minimum recommendation, if you see fit, and we don't quarrel with the minimum recommendation of half of the appropriate term. So if the term remains at 20 years, I don't suggest that a minimum term of ten is unfair. If it were reduced to 15, I would say the period should be seven and a half by way of illustration. I'm content with the percentage, but we do submit, as a matter of fundamental principle and fairness, the time ought to run from when the appellant first lost his liberty because he has, in reality, been a prisoner throughout. Third, another feature that we say is fundamentally unfair, is that from, I believe, February 1994 to the 24th of April of 1995, a period of 14 months, the appellant was in custody in the Federal Republic of Germany. He was only in custody, as I understand it, in relation to allegations that were embraced in the facts heard by the Trial Chamber. It is set out at paragraph 6 of the judgement: "Dusko Tadic was arrested in February 1994 in Germany, where he was then living, on suspicion of having committed offences at the Omarska camp in the former Yugoslavia in June 1992, including torture and aiding and abetting the commission of genocide, which constitute crimes under German law." Now, of course I accept that technically he was in the custody of a foreign state but, in reality, he was in custody for these offences because it was the investigation into that very camp that occupied the time of the Trial Chamber, and it is, so far as the appellant is concerned, of course, of little comfort to him that he has spent 14 months in the prison of another state before being transferred here in relation to exactly the same offences. The Trial Chamber found as a fact that both sets of investigations involved the same crimes; and therefore, we submit that in all fairness to him, credit must be given for that period in custody. It has expressly not been given so far. It was time when his liberty had been deprived, it had been deprived for these offences, and this Appeals Chamber has the power to revise the sentence to give him that credit. It amounts to 14 months which, if one equates that with the 50 per cent minimum period, would reduce the minimum recommendation by 28 months and the sentence likewise. I hope I have explained that adequately. You have got to factor in the benefit which would otherwise not be given. The Court will, of course, be aware, under Rule 101, it says there that: "Credit shall be given to the convicted person for the period, if any, during which the convicted person was detained in custody pending surrender to the Tribunal or pending trial or appeal." Of course, here he was in custody having been charged with offences in Germany, so he was technically in custody in relation to a wholly separate jurisdiction, and it was only when arrangements were made for the transfer that he was then brought over and placed in the detention of the United Nations. But it is, with respect, rather academic so far as the impact on the prisoner is concerned, it is of no benefit to him to be in prison in Germany as opposed to being in prison in The Hague. He has been in prison throughout, and we would submit that it would be an injustice if he were not to be given credit for that time. Unless I can assist the Chamber any further, those are our submissions on sentence. The Court will, of course, have seen the transcripts and there are reports and psychiatric reports and the like. We rely upon all of those, but I don't wish to bring them expressly to the Court's attention. I say nothing, of course, about the possible cooperation. If there is any benefit to be gained from that, it will be gained as a result of submissions in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, one question. My impression is that somewhere in the judgement there is a reference to this provision requiring the Court to have regard to the sentencing practice of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, 24(1). Am I right that the Court below construed that to mean that the Court was required to take account of the sentencing practice in Yugoslavia without being bound by that sentencing practice? Do you have any submissions to make on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I don't dissent from that interpretation of the Rules by the Trial Chamber. We would submit they took insufficient account of the sentencing practice, but I don't think I could argue that they were bound by it because it would seem to me to be a conclusion that was contrary to the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. One last question, it arises under Rule 101(D) which you read out to us, and it concerns the period during which the prisoner was held in the Federal Republic of Germany. Would you say that that period was a period when he was detained in custody pending surrender to the Tribunal, that is to say, before a request for deferral had been made?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Well, I think technically he probably wasn't. He was actually in custody pending trial in Germany. It wasn't until the request for referral was made that he then was pending surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Your arguments rest then on the factual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. It is October '94 when they ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Clegg. Then we would hear from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution position on sentence is that the sentence in this case was in accordance with the law, that it was appropriate to the crimes and to the offender, that it was determined after a consideration of the matters required to be considered by Rule 101 and by Article 41(1) of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia, and it should not be disturbed on appeal. In terms of this principle of hierarchy of relative criminal culpability, at paragraph 60 and 70 of its decision, the Trial Chamber took into account the accused's position within opstina Prijedor compared to others and also took on this general idea about this hierarchy of relative criminal culpability, so it did consider that argument in arriving at its determination of a just sentence. It pointed out, we suggest very appropriately, that you cannot have this strict hierarchy because you would be looking at this speculation about what would be done in other cases that have yet to be tried and yet to be found guilty and yet to be sentenced. We would suggest that a strict hierarchical approach would also be in opposition to this theory that you have to sentence an accused based not just on the crimes but also on the individual circumstances of each accused. Nonetheless, the Trial Chamber took this principle into consideration, applied it to Mr. Tadic, and arrived at a sentence they believed to be appropriate after such consideration. We suggest that that was not at all an inappropriate sentence in light of that principle. First of all, the Trial Chamber had at its disposal the possibility of a maximum sentence of imprisonment for the remainder of the accused's life. The Trial Chamber also had at its disposal the possibility of imposition of consecutive sentences. The Trial Chamber chose neither of those options and, indeed, sentenced this accused to 20 years' confinement and sentenced him to serve his sentences concurrently. It did, in fact, look at a much reduced sentence to those options that were available to it. It was not an abuse of discretion for the Trial Chamber to have arrived at this decision on sentencing, and we suggest this is a standard that needs to be applied here. The appellant has conceded that the language "have recourse to" is not binding, and indeed that is consistent with the jurisprudence that has developed in both this Tribunal and the Rwanda Tribunal which has the identical language in regard to penalties. In addition, there was no violation of any law, even in the existing Code in Bosnia-Herzegovina, by an imposition of 20 years. Twenty years was not binding, and at all times relevant to these offences and these proceedings, it was still possible in Bosnia-Herzegovina to, in fact, have imposed the death penalty for crimes similar to that which the accused was convicted of. In addition to that, in the International Community, it is accepted that where states are now disallowing the death penalty, they may impose the alternative punishment of life imprisonment. It is also accepted in the International Community that crimes such as this appellant was convicted of, including crimes against humanity, are viewed as to be among the most serious of offences that can be committed. The imposition of the 20-year sentence, therefore, was within the permissible, lawful limits available to the Trial Chamber. The sentence is not excessive either. It is within the discretion of the Trial Chamber to determine what sentence is appropriate to the offender and to the offence. The Trial Chamber considered all the factors that were set forth and required by this Court's Rules and also that were set forth in the Code of the former Yugoslavia. After looking at those factors, the Trial Chamber came up with its decision. The Trial Chamber also noted the purposes of sentencing and that sentence must not only fit the crime but also the offender. In arriving at its decision, the Trial Chamber noted not just the personal circumstances of the accused, including the existence of this propaganda campaign and the impact it may have had on people, it also considered that the accused took part in this propaganda campaign. It considered circumstances that were relevant to this particular accused, but it also considered the brutality of the acts that the accused himself engaged in. It considered his willingness to become part of this comprehensive ethnic cleansing in opstina Prijedor. It considered also his conscious desire to contribute to the elimination of non-Serbs in Prijedor and his involvement in beatings that resulted in death and other very severe and brutal crimes. When we look at what the Trial Chamber decided in this case, we suggest to you that this sentence is not excessive because in toto what we have is an accused who willingly and enthusiastically participated in the entire scope of ethnic cleansing in opstina Prijedor impacting the entire opstina, people killed, people brutally tortured and beaten, people forced from their homes, from their relatives, from their livelihoods, from life as they knew it, and to death and exile. Twenty years is not excessive for that. It is not an abuse of discretion. Turning to the additional point that the Defence raised concerning the minimum sentence recommendation, we suggest to you that that was entirely appropriate and helpful. First of all, this Trial Chamber determined in its ability to adjudge a sentence that the appropriate sentence for this accused would be to be in gaol for 20 years -- 20 years. However, the Trial Chamber was also properly mindful that when the accused was actually sent to serve his confinement, that the laws of the country where he served that confinement could produce the possibility of parole or other relief from the sentence. The Trial Chamber was exercising its right as the fact-finders who sat through this entire case, who had the benefit of seeing all of the witnesses, who had the benefit of observing this accused, including his testimony, observing his demeanour, evaluating him and his acts. They had the right to recommend how much of the 20-year sentence should be served before grace was given to this accused, and that is what this minimum recommendation is. The Trial Chamber is telling whoever it will be who will act upon a recommendation for grace that, in this Trial Chamber's opinion, based on their observations, the minimum that this accused owes to society for his wrongs, considering his circumstances and his crimes, is ten years plus the time he has been in confinement awaiting his trial and awaiting the appeal. That is not an improper recommendation. It is an appropriate recommendation from the most appropriate, impartial body that could provide it, and we recommend that you not disturb that recommendation. In terms of credit for time spent in confinement in Germany, the Trial Chamber, we suggest, complied fully with the requirements of the Rule. Should this Appellate Chamber determine first that the Rule is unjust, certainly the Appellate Chamber has the ability to change it. We would suggest the Rule is not unjust. It is not uncommon in many jurisdictions for an accused to be given credit only for the time that he spent in confinement in that particular jurisdiction or awaiting trial in that particular jurisdiction. So this is not in opposite to existing rules of criminal law. Should this Appellate Chamber determine that the Trial Chamber imposed the wrong date as the beginning of his confinement in Germany awaiting trial here or awaiting transfer, that is for the Appellate Chamber to determine. We submit that the Trial Chamber applied the Rule appropriately, and we request that you not disturb that on appeal. We submit to you, finally, that this sentence is appropriate, that it certainly is not excessive, that it is far below the maximum that could have been imposed, that this appellant, by his wilful, enthusiastic actions and choices, deserves this punishment, after taking consideration of his personal circumstances. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, one little point. Perhaps I didn't understand you correctly. I heard you to be saying something to this effect, and I'm translating here, that if the Trial Chamber felt that Rule 101 was unjust, the Trial Chamber had the power to change the Rule. Did I hear you correctly on that point?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I had attempted to say is that on appeal, if the Appellate Chamber believes that this Rule is unfair, would result in an unfair sentence, that the Appellate Chamber has the authority and the power to change the Rule. I would suggest to you that if a Trial Chamber determines that any Rule would deprive an accused of a fair trial or would prevent a fair decision on sentence, that even a Trial Chamber would have the ability to strike down the Rule, because the ultimate requirement, of course, is that there is a fair trial, and we would suggest that that includes a fair proceeding and a fair judgement on sentence. The point that I was trying to make is that if, in this Appeals Chamber's determination, this Rule, as it is presently written, would deprive an appellant of a fair determination of sentence and credit towards sentence, of course, this Appellate Chamber has the authority to change that Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. I understand you then to mean that if the Appeals Chamber were to hold that the operation of Rule 101 would collide with the mandate of the Tribunal to ensure fairness under the Statute, then the Appeals Chamber would have the right to strike down the Rule; am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, but we would suggest that it would have to rise to that level. It would be a deprivation of a fundamental fairness, not that it would be a substitution of judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Clegg, we have you down lastly for a maximum of 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I think the Court can be confident that I will not be occupying anything like that long. As to the general principle of whether the sentence of 20 years was an unfair sentence or not, I'm not suggesting that the Trial Chamber didn't have drawn to their attention the appropriate factors for them to take into account. The effect of the sentence is, we submit, nonetheless unfair. The Trial Chamber was working in a vacuum in passing sentence in this case. There was no other person that had ever been convicted. It was faced with a formidable task which it, doubtless, strived as hard as it could to conclude in a manner consistent with fairness. It is our submission that, upon analysis, it failed to do so. The question of the tariff and pitching the sentence of the appellant in a bracket that will enable the Tribunal in future to deal fairly with other accused is not a matter, we submit, of speculation. One knows that there are others who have been indicted by this Tribunal who are clearly decision-makers, who have clearly formulated policy, and one has to bear in mind the relative culpability of different people in order to achieve justice. I am not suggesting there was anything wrong in the Trial Chamber specifying a minimum period of ten years. It's a perfectly reasonable recommendation for them to have made, pitching it at 50 per cent of the determinate sentence. What I am suggesting is clearly unfair is to leave the starting date wholly uncertain. I venture to suggest that not one of the members of the Trial Chamber would have been as pessimistic enough to imagine that today would be the last day of the appeal hearing before judgement two years after they had delivered their judgement. They effectively issued a minimum recommendation with no idea of when it would start. That must be fundamentally unfair. In our submission, the only fair starting date for a minimum recommendation must be the date when one loses one's liberty. That's when everything runs from. It's when your sentence runs from; likewise, so the minimum recommendation. Finally, can I just deal with the question of credit being given and the impact of Rule 101? I agree with Ms. Hollis's view of the law in relation to that. If she says that she knows of jurisdictions where there is no credit given for time served in another jurisdiction whilst awaiting trial, then I certainly don't dispute her knowledge. It's superior to mine. Certainly, in the field of extradition, it is always the case that credit is given in the country which receives the person who has been extradited for time spent in custody awaiting extradition in the state where the application was made, and I feel cautiously optimistic that, under the European Convention, if one of the member states did not give such credit, then I'm cautiously optimistic that the European Court would overturn any such decision. I cannot, I'm afraid, off the top of my head think of a case where that has actually occurred, but certainly throughout Europe, the practice is for credit to be given in extradition cases, and it would seem to me to be in contravention of the European Convention were it not to be. My understanding was that certainly interstate in America, there is always credit given. I don't think if you're arrested in Arizona, you don't get your credit if your trial happens to be in Nevada. I'm not saying that there isn't somewhere a jurisdiction where that doesn't apply, but it certainly isn't a practice that I would recommend, with respect, to the Appeals Chamber. Unless I can assist the Appeals Chamber any further, that is our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just one point. I thought you spoke of time spent in custody awaiting extradition, and your argument was that credit was given for such time. Is that position very different from the position which I understood Ms. Hollis to be presenting, that if you are, in fact, held in another country -- in fact, held in another country -- pending surrender to the Tribunal, you are eligible for credit for that period. The dispute is whether you are eligible for credit for any prior period in which, as in this case, you were held in custody but not pending surrender to the Tribunal. You see, there was a period when the appellant was held in Germany --

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- solely for the purposes of criminal proceedings in Germany itself, and then came the Tribunal with a deferral order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The extradition case is not a perfect analogy. There are certainly cases where a person is arrested in relation to crimes allegedly committed domestically, and, thereafter, an application is made in relation to extradition because those offences embrace crimes of an international character that are more conveniently to be tried in another state. In those circumstances, certainly in England, credit would be given for the time that you were held in custody in relation to the offences then going to be tried in the national courts of the other country. Certainly insofar as England is concerned, credit would be given for that. I think the approach would be that the prisoner has been in custody for those offences, and it is really rather academic as to where the trial is going to take place. The important thing to concentrate on is how long has the prisoner lost his liberty for? I am not competent to be able to say whether that would apply throughout the regions covered by the European Convention, I suspect that it probably would, but it may be that others in this room will know that much better than I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: There are no further questions, Mr. Clegg. Thank you. Does that conclude the hearing in this matter? Are there any other points which have been overlooked?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Not for the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Not for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well then, the position is that I would, on behalf of the Bench, like to thank learned counsel on both sides for the excellent assistance which they have afforded the Bench in this matter. We will retire to deliberate. We will reserve our judgement and we will indicate a date in due course when the judgement will be delivered. What I will say is that there is no risk of that happening before the time periods agreed on this morning will have expired, that is, seven days (sic) plus 14 days, that will happen. And if, if, perchance the Court were to agree with the Prosecution in its appeal against acquittal, then there will be a separate sentencing procedure. I think that ends the appeal proper. A request has reached me from Mr. Livingston about a related but separate matter, and it would be appropriate if we were to go into private session so as to enable him to make his request. Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Let me take the opportunity to correct my mathematics. I said the Prosecution had seven days. Mr. Hocking has just pointed out that I was in grievous error. I short-changed the Prosecution by three days. The Prosecution has ten days and the Defence 14 days. (Private session)
